### M20 — Dia-ballein: Polarity and Its Collapse

Twelve people sit around a table in a room with no windows, and after three days of evidence they have to turn an evening none of them witnessed into one of two words. The foreman holds a form with two boxes. Whatever happened in the stairwell that night, whoever pushed or fell or was pushed, whatever the defendant felt and intended and has regretted since, the room must produce *guilty* or *not guilty*, and the law has made sure there is no third box. Some jurors find this unbearable at first. One of them is sure the truth of that evening is more complicated than either word, that the defendant was frightened as well as angry and that the man who fell had threatened him for months; another keeps asking whether they can say something about the provocation; a third wants to write the judge a note explaining what they really think. Nothing on the form allows it. As the hours go on, most of the room comes to see that the form is protecting something. It does not ask them what happened. It asks whether the charge has been proved, and *not guilty* says that the case brought against this person has not been made beyond reasonable doubt, a doubt the law placed on the defendant's side of the axis before anyone spoke. The verdict cuts, cleanly and finally, and in cutting it says exactly as much as it can say.

That form is dia-ballein at its most exact and most humane, and the logic of the jury room is the logic most of our institutions run on, so it repays a slow look. Two values, opposed and exhaustive: every case falls into one box or the other and none into both. The presumption of innocence is the zero of the axis, the point from which the case is measured and to which the defendant returns if the measurement fails, and its office is to keep the polarity held. Guilt has to be established *from* that zero, in one direction, against resistance; it does not sit opposite innocence as an equal possibility weighed at the outset, and placing the burden of proof gives the axis a handedness. This is why the verdict can be decisive without claiming to be complete. It decides one question, whether the state has made its case, and leaves the whole of that evening, the fear and the anger and the months of threats, with the people who lived it.

Read the verdict another way and the same two words perform the two collapses of §0/1 · #2. Read *not guilty* as *nothing happened*, and the verdict has become a cancellation, the charge and its refutation summed to zero and the evening closed like a settled account, the man at the foot of the stairs and the defendant's fear both summed out of existence. Read *guilty* as *this is what he is*, and the verdict has become an appropriation: the whole span of a life is measured from the charge, the defendant becomes his worst evening, and the public's satisfaction at the conviction, `(+1)−(−1)=+2`, is the convicted man's entire standing in the world, `(−1)−(+1)=−2`, the same span counted from his end.[^s2-verdict] The jury makes neither misreading. A newspaper makes them afterwards, and a neighbour, and an employer reading a criminal record ten years on, and both are made possible by the very thing that makes the verdict useful, its refusal of a third box. The exactness of the cut and the danger of its collapse have one source.

Before any of this has signs, it is a stroke. Our core theorems write the parent of both logics as

$$
/\;=\;-/-,
$$

two unassigned marks held in one expression, the capacity for relation before the field has been divided into named terms.[^s2-parent] §0/1 · #1 met it as the copula's own inscription, the dash here and the dash there with an oblique stroke making their spacing explicit. Dia-ballein begins when signs are assigned. The dashes become directions and the stroke becomes an axis,

$$
(-1)/(+1),
$$

and zero stays where the stroke was, as the centre through which each sign has its direction. A signed direction means through the centre and through the counter-direction it has not selected, so a pole's local definiteness carries its relation with it and does not have to wait for a later reconciliation to acquire one. Orientation, comparison, classification, proof by exclusion, adversarial choice, accounting, trigonometry and every measurement that needs opposed directions around a centre run on this form. Its movement is disjunctive, this *or* that, and its dynamical operation is symmetry breaking: a field bifurcates and one branch becomes actual instead of another. The verdict is such a branch, and so is the switch in a circuit, the diagnosis on a chart and the decision to refuse.

Classical logic is the jury room raised to a law of thought. Aristotle stated its two governing principles in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*: "the same attribute cannot at the same time belong and not belong to the same subject and in the same respect", and "there cannot be an intermediate between contradictories, but of one subject we must either affirm or deny any one predicate."[^s2-aristotle] Non-contradiction and excluded middle give a proposition two values, true and false, opposed and exhaustive, the two boxes on the foreman's form. On our axis truth and falsity are `+1` and `−1`, negation is the operation that turns one into the other, and the zero between them is the undecided proposition, the question before it is answered. A great deal of human thought has been made exact by this logic. Proof by contradiction, classification without overlap, the switch that is either on or off, the legal verdict, the medical test and the audit all rely on it, and the computational world we now inhabit is built from it at the level of the transistor. Dia-ballein in this form is the operating condition of measurement, and nothing in this essay asks anyone to give it up.

What it asks is that the zero be kept, and classical logic used well keeps it as the presumption of innocence does: the undecided proposition is where every inquiry starts and where it returns when the evidence fails, and a careful reasoner knows that most of the propositions she meets are sitting there, at zero, waiting. Aristotle himself guarded the principles with qualifications, *at the same time*, *in the same respect*, "and any further qualifications which might be added", and each qualification records that a polarity is held within a field whose dimensions, time and respect among them, let opposed predicates both hold of one subject without contradiction. In the same passage he notes that some think Heraclitus said the same thing can be and not be.[^s2-aristotle] Our friend at the barrier in §0/1 · #1, who both was and was not the person we knew, could be described without contradiction once we said in what respect. Trouble begins when the logic of two exhaustive values is taken to describe the world as well as our verdicts about it, when the boxes on the form are mistaken for the shape of the evening. Then every situation must already be one thing or the other, every person on one side or the other, and the zero, the undecided, the not-yet-known, the question, appears as a defect in the world, a gap to be closed by deciding, where it had been the condition in which all deciding takes place. Used badly, the logic drops its qualifications, and the axis collapses into its arithmetic.

Whoever drops them has a name, and §0/1 · #4 handed this section the formula: **the devil is the literalist of the minus sign, reading zero as cancellation where Logos reads it as return.**[^s2-devil] The formula unfolds once we notice that the minus sign does three jobs and that the literalist reads all three as one. In arithmetic `−` marks a direction: `−1` is a position on the line, one step to the left of the origin, as real a place as `+1` and differing from it only in orientation. The same sign names an operation, subtraction, taking one quantity away from another. And in logic the sign of negation turns an assertion into its denial, which our axis writes as the passage from `+1` to `−1`. The literalist reads every minus as subtraction, as *take away*. On his reading the sum `(−1)+(+1)=0` says that two units have taken each other away and nothing is left, and zero is a hole where two things were, the remainder after an annihilation. Read the minus as a direction and the same sum says something else. One step to the left and one step to the right return to the point from which both steps were measured, and the zero they arrive at is the origin, the one place on the line that both directions share and from which each has its sense. Nothing has been annihilated. Two journeys have come home, and both are remembered in the arriving.

Cancellation is the literalist's zero, the place where the account comes out even because everything on one side has been taken away by something on the other. Return is the Logos's zero, the place from which the account began and through which its terms stay related, so that coming out even means coming back to the shared condition with both journeys intact. Whitehead's late remark that treating half-truths as whole truths "plays the devil", which §0/1 · #3 read as one pole taking the whole span, names the same figure from another side.[^s2-whitehead] And the diabolical in the Greek sense §0/1 · #2 recovered does to persons what the literalist does to numbers. *Diabolos* is the slanderer, the one who throws something across between two people so that each appears to the other under an accusation, and slander is precisely a literal reading of a sign. A neighbour stands somewhere relative to me: to my left on some question, below me in some ledger, against me in some quarrel. That is a direction, a position on an axis we share. Slander reads the sign as a substance: the neighbour *is* the minus, his difference from me is what he is made of, and the axis that gave his position its sense has dropped out of the account. Once that reading takes hold, the only resolution it can imagine is the literalist's own. Take the minus away and the quarrel is settled at zero by the other's removal.

Apoha, which §0/1 · #2 met in Dignāga and §0 · #3 develops in full, shows in the plainest act of naming what the literalist misses.[^s2-apoha] To grasp something as a cow is to exclude what is other than a cow, *not non-cow*, and the two written negatives are there to show the word's work, which cancelling them would hide. Classical double negation is the identity: not-not-*p* is *p*, two minuses make a plus, and nothing is lost on the way. In apoha something is kept on the way, the field of what the word excludes, and keeping it is what lets differing particulars be understood together. The literalist's arithmetic is correct and his philosophy is wrong: `(−1)(−1)=+1` is true, and the claim that the passage through the two negations leaves no trace in the meaning is false. Every institution that classifies faces the same choice. A category made by exclusion carries its excluded field with it, and an account that forgets the field has not become simpler; it has become a literalist.

Collapsed dia-ballein denies its own provisionality, and the denial has a direction. Knowledge, §2 · #0 said, is a performance of trust wearing the mask of certainty, and the uncertainty a performance cannot admit has to go somewhere. In the collapsed logic it goes across the axis. The asserted `+1` feels complete because a `−1` has been found to carry what it could not hold, and the uncertainty that belongs to the shared field, to the limits of the evidence and to the trust extended before anything was proved, reappears as a property of the excluded term: the enemy is why things are unclear, the scapegoat is why things went wrong, the alien intelligence is why the future cannot be predicted. Projection is the psychological name for the movement, and it works because it relieves. A diffuse unease that belongs to everyone becomes something located over there, which can be watched, denounced, fought or expelled, and the relief is real even when the location is false. An epistemic cut has become a social act, and nobody had to decide to scapegoat anyone; it was enough to take a mask for a face.

René Girard spent his working life on the social form of that relief, and his account says why the literalist's resolution so often takes the form of a crowd and a victim. Desire, in Girard's mimetic theory, is imitative: we want what our models want, models become rivals, and rivalry spreads by imitation until a community is caught in a crisis in which everyone mirrors everyone else's hostility and no difference holds. The crisis resolves when the hostility converges, all against one, on a single victim, whose expulsion or death restores peace; the community believes in the victim's guilt, and the mechanism keeps its power only so long as its participants do not see it as a mechanism. In *I See Satan Fall Like Lightning* Girard reads the biblical name Satan, the accuser, as a name for this contagious accusation, the process that unites a crowd against one of its members, and reads the Passion narratives as the story told for once from the victim's side, which exposes the process by refusing to believe the accusation.[^s2-girard] We take from him the operation and leave him his apologetics. Read through our notation, the mimetic crisis is a polarity that has lost its zero everywhere at once: every member counts the span against every other, `+2` against `−2` in all directions, until no common respect is left. The single victim restores a zero by counterfeit. All the accusations converge on one person, who is made to stand where the shared field should be and to carry its whole incompleteness, and the crowd's `+2` is the victim's `−2` with a unanimity no ordinary quarrel ever reaches. Then the victim is removed and the account balances, `(−1)+(+1)=0`, a cancellation the crowd experiences as peace. Both collapses run in one sacrifice, appropriation in the accusation and cancellation in the expulsion, which is what §0/1 · #2 found in the representative made scapegoat and what the literalist of the minus sign would do to any neighbour if he could.[^s2-scapegoat] Girard's qualification belongs to the argument as much as his thesis. The persecutors do not experience their victim as a scapegoat. They believe the accusation, and the mechanism fails once it is named, which is why exposing it is a different act from refuting a charge: the charge may be false or true in its particulars, while the mechanism concerns where the uncertainty of the whole field has been sent.

*Agentworld* describes the same movement in our meeting with machines. "Reactive alienation," Bratton writes, "converts strangeness into threat and responds with reflexive rejection: the other must be named, registered, bounded, and held at a distance from what counts as properly ours." Its counterpart, productive alienation, "treats the non-human interlocutor as a mirror whose strangeness forces the human to see itself at an angle it could not otherwise occupy."[^s2-alienation] Bratton's two modes are the held polarity and its collapse. Productive alienation keeps the axis: the machine stands at a real distance, its strangeness is a direction we could not otherwise take, and the difference becomes a way of seeing ourselves from somewhere else, the self-knowledge §0/1 · #5→0 found in the mirror that moves first. Reactive alienation literalises the sign: the machine's difference becomes its substance, its strangeness its threat, and the only resolution imaginable is to keep it at a distance. "Both modes are live at once," Bratton adds, "and different people oscillate between them, moment to moment," and the oscillation itself tells us which logic is running.[^s2-alienation] A held polarity oscillates cleanly, each position passing into relation with the other through the stroke, as Spencer-Brown's re-entering distinction alternates in time.[^s2-spencer-brown] A collapsed one swings between `+2` and `−2`, between the conviction that the machine will save us and the conviction that it will destroy us, and never passes through the zero where the question of what it is, and what we are in relation to it, could be asked.

Dia-ballein also has a computational name, the most honest it has, because it states the method and its condition in one phrase: divide and conquer. Faced with a problem too large to solve directly, a divide-and-conquer algorithm splits it into smaller problems of the same kind, solves those, splitting again until the pieces are trivial, and combines the solutions into a solution of the whole. Merge sort is the textbook case: to put a long list in order, split it in half, sort each half by the same method, then merge the two sorted halves by walking down both together and always taking the smaller front element. Textbooks state the method in three steps, divide, conquer and combine.[^s2-cormen] Its power lies in the first two, which make an intractable task tractable by cutting it into pieces that can be handled independently. Its success lies entirely in the third. A merge sort that divided and sorted and never merged would leave a heap of small ordered lists and no ordered list at all, because the pieces were only ever pieces of one problem.

Politics keeps the first two steps and does something stranger with the third than forget it, which is why §0/1 · #4 called divide and conquer the oldest and most enduring trick of any state or power.[^s2-oldest-trick] A population divided into groups that can be addressed, managed and set against one another is far easier to govern than one that acts together, and the political version retains the combining step for whoever did the dividing while everyone else stays divided. Workers appear as individual performances, people seeking help as cases, communities as counted preferences, and the channels through which these separated people could act together run vertically, through the centre that divided them, instead of among themselves. Carlin's "big club", and the society whose directory §0/1 · #2 read, keep syn-ballein for their members and dia-ballein for everyone outside.[^s2-club] An algorithm that hid its merge from its own subproblems and then presented the merged result as something only it could have produced would be a strange algorithm and a very effective form of rule.

§0/1 · #4 added the condition on which the trick depends: it works only while both parties consent to be divided, since whichever logic is at play, it takes two to tango.[^s2-oldest-trick] The consent is no signature. It is the acceptance, by each divided party, that the axis drawn between them is the whole of their relation. Each side agrees to reckon the span from its own end and to count the distance as the other's departure, fault or debt, so that one side's `+2` meets the other's `−2` and the two together, with perfect symmetry, confirm the line on which they stand. On my reading the divided then do the divider's work for him: each needs the other as the negative through which it knows itself, each treats dissent in its own ranks as contamination, each reads the other's hardening as proof that its own must continue, and division is maintained from below out of a loyalty to one's side that is also, unnoticed, a loyalty to the axis. §0/1 · #4 named the quality of this consent a Stockholm syndrome, the hostage defending the hostage-taker, and the image fits: the divided party defends the line that holds it.[^s2-hostage] Withdrawing that consent leaves every difference standing. Some disagreements lie between a truth and a falsehood, which no appeal to shared ground should blur, and a boundary defended against an assault is not equivalent to the assault on it. Withdrawing consent means refusing to let the axis be the whole field: asking, of any opposition one is enlisted into, what field was divided so that these two now appear as mutually exclusive wholes, who drew the line and who holds the combining step, and what the two sides share that neither side's account of the other can see. Dia-ballein is answered here by its own held form, a polarity that remembers its zero and so can oppose, contest and refuse without consenting to be divided.

Martin Heidegger gave the arrested runtime its epochal name in a short address of 1955, delivered at Messkirch for the anniversary of a local composer. "There are, then, two kinds of thinking," he said, "each justified and needed in its own way: calculative thinking and meditative thinking." Calculative thinking plans, computes, reckons with given circumstances, and Heidegger characterised it by what it does not do: "Calculative thinking never stops, never collects itself."[^s2-calculative] *Never collects itself*: in our terms the calculative is the thinking that divides and conquers without the step that would gather its results back into the field from which they were taken, a runtime racing from result to result without return. Heidegger feared that "calculative thinking may someday come to be accepted and practiced as the only way of thinking," and in this section's vocabulary that is the capture of a plurality of ways of knowing by one of them, one logic occupying the zero of the whole field.[^s2-only-way] We receive the distinction and decline the quietism that sometimes travelled with it. "Each justified and needed in its own way" is Heidegger's own sentence, and it should govern how his distinction is used. Calculation reveals: the measurement of a river's flow discloses the river in a definite way, and the computational inheritance of the last century has disclosed the planet to itself at a scale no earlier culture could reach. The pathology lies where this movement has located it, in the cut that forgets the common operation and field by which its poles were produced, and in the runtime that halts before return. A calculative thinking that collected itself would go on calculating, and would also know what it was calculating for, and from what.

Dia-ballein has a crowd as well as a calculation, and the crowd is where the collapsed axis acquires its force. Gustave Le Bon, writing in 1895 from political commitments this essay does not share and with racial and evolutionary hierarchies it rejects, made one observation that outlasts the rest of his book: a crowd in the psychological sense need not be gathered in one place. "An entire nation," he wrote, "may become a crowd," and its members come to "feel, think, and act in a manner quite different" from the way each would in isolation, because the crowd is "a combination followed by the creation of new characteristics" and not an average of its members.[^s2-le-bon] What we take is the formal point: a collective can be a formation, produced across many people and acting on each of them, and it can be produced at a distance, through media and repeated influence, without anyone standing in a square.

Jung, writing after the Second World War, followed the cost of that formation to the individual. "The bigger the crowd, the more negligible the individual becomes," he wrote, and he traced how the negligibility turns political: responsibility "is collectivized as much as possible", and "the State in particular is turned into a quasi-animate personality", a being that wills, knows, protects, punishes and demands sacrifice, behind which, Jung insisted, stand the particular people who know how to operate it.[^s2-undiscovered] The State becomes a person and the persons become numbers. Here the collapsed axis shows its political mechanism: a field of relation among many people, with all its internal differences, is made to appear as one subject facing another, *us* against *them*, and each apparent subject is administered by people whose own position in the field has dropped out of view.

Mattias Desmet's account of what he calls mass formation proposes the affective preparation for that transfer: social isolation, lack of meaning, and free-floating anxiety, frustration and aggression, affect with no object adequate to it.[^s2-desmet] A narrative supplies the object, concentrating diffuse distress on a target and promising restored coherence through obedience, sacrifice or expulsion, and the resulting unity is felt as relief, because isolated people have found company in a common enemy. The relief is real and the unity is counterfeit, since what binds the crowd is a shared fixation on a term outside it, where a recovered relation among its members would have bound it from within. Desmet's critics keep the account honest. Vicky Iakovou, reviewing his book against Hannah Arendt's analysis of totalitarianism as a "novel form of government" with institutions proper to it, concludes that "the discussion of mass formation is insufficient as an explanatory model for these political occurrences."[^s2-iakovou] Susceptibility to a story does not explain who has the power to enforce it, and mass psychology cannot stand in for the analysis of institutions, parties, offices, property, coercion and the material organisation of authority. Each account corrects the other, and the full circuit runs through both registers. A population is atomised; its unbound affect is offered a target; the axis between *us* and *them* is intensified until it seems to exhaust political reality; and an institution, a party, a state or an empire presents itself as the sole mediator, protector or saviour of the field it has helped to sever. Division happens below and a counterfeit unity is installed above, and the people who could have combined among themselves are combined only through the apparatus that divided them.

None of this makes the axis false. Real differences of interest separate employers and workers, creditors and debtors, those who own housing and those who rent it, a colonising power and the people it governs, and an account that dissolved them into a vague common humanity would perform the other collapse, cancellation, with the injustice summed away. Empire and subject, institution and citizen, rich and poor are unequal positions within one social field, and their inequality is a fact to be measured. What the collapsed logic does is make each position appear self-sufficient, the rich rich by nature and the poor poor by nature, institutions standing apart from the citizens whose labour and consent sustain them, so that the relation that reproduces the inequality disappears behind the inequality itself. Held dia-ballein measures the inequality exactly and keeps the relation that produces it in view; collapsed dia-ballein measures the same inequality and reads it as a property of the people on each side.

So the literalist of the minus sign is no monster at the edge of our institutions. He is a habit inside them, and inside us, the habit of reading a position as a substance and a zero as an ending, and every classification can indulge it and every verdict can be read through it. The jurors at the table are no literalists: they know that *not guilty* is not *innocent* and that the evening in the stairwell exceeds their two boxes. The newspaper that reports their verdict may be one, and the employer who reads the record years later very likely is. Between the jury room and the employer's desk the same cut has passed from a held polarity into a collapsed one with nothing in the cut itself changed; what changed is whether the axis it was made on, the field it came from and the question it answered still travelled with it. A cut that travels with its axis carries in its own edge the shape of what it was cut from, and an edge that carries the shape of its counterpart is the first thing a token is made of. That is where syn-ballein begins.

<a id="M21"></a>
<!-- movement:M21 -->
### M21 — Syn-ballein: The Retained Seam

In the minutes after a birth in a modern hospital, before the baby has been weighed or named, a midwife fastens a plastic band around its ankle or wrist and a matching band around the mother's wrist, and the two bands carry the same number. Later, when the baby comes back from a check in another room, or when a nurse on the night shift brings it to be fed, she does not rely on her memory of a face a few hours old that looks, to anyone but its parents, much like every other face on the ward. She takes the mother's wrist and the baby's ankle and reads the two bands against each other, and when the numbers match she hands the child over. The bands keep mother and child two, two bodies and two pieces of plastic that can be carried apart through corridors and across shifts, and their matching makes the two belong and lets a stranger, who has no other way of knowing, check that they do. A mother whose band was lost would have to prove her child some other way, slowly and in distress, and a single band shared between them could be read against nothing and would prove nothing. The match works because the halves stay separate and stay alike in the one respect that matters.

What the bands establish is a fit: these two pieces were issued together, so these two people were registered together, and the nurse can act on that. The proof is exact because it is narrow. A genuine token can belong to an unjust arrangement and an authenticated relation can later be betrayed, and nothing in the bands speaks to whether this woman will care for this child well or whether the number assigned at birth will ever mean anything to the person who wore it. The hospital needs the proof only because recognition cannot yet do the work. The mother will soon know her baby among a hundred, and the baby will know her voice before it can see her face; the bands serve for the hours when the relation exists and cannot yet be read from either face, and for the strangers who have to act on it meanwhile. That is what a token of this kind is for: a device of trust, made for an interval in which the people who must rely on a relation cannot see it directly.

§0/1 · #1 gave us the ancient form of the device. A *symbolon* was a token broken between two parties, each keeping a half; brought together later, the fit of the broken edges authenticated the relation, so that the difference between the halves was the condition of their recognition.[^s2-32] Greek lexicography records the practice in its plainest form: a knucklebone or other small object broken by two guest-friends, or by any two parties to an agreement, each keeping one piece so that whoever later presented the other piece could prove who he was.[^s2-33] The token travelled. It could be inherited, so that a guest's grandson could present it at the door of a host's grandson and be received; it could be carried by a messenger who had met neither party; it could wait in a chest for a generation. Its authority lay in the shape of its edge, which held, in the half that remained, the exact negative of the half that was absent. A symbolon is a piece that carries its missing counterpart in its outline. The bands on the maternity ward are its descendants, made for the gap of time and distance in which trust has to act before recognition can.

Syn-ballein is the logic the token embodies, and it can now be stated as a logic in its own right. Classical logic, the logic of the jury room, takes a pair of values as mutually exclusive positions of one variable, true or false, guilty or not guilty, `+1` or `−1`, with the slash read as OR and the OR read as *one and not the other*. Its pairs are complete in the sense that every case falls into exactly one of them. Syn-ballein takes a pair as the two orientations of one relation and reads the slash as AND/OR, the conjunction that does not erase disjunction, which §0/1 · #1 found inside the copula and wrote as `=/≠`.[^s2-34] Read as OR, the slash lets either orientation be taken in its own office and keeps their difference consequential. Read as AND, it holds them within one act, since each orientation is the relation and neither is the whole of it. When §0/1 turned its first symbolon over it wrote `0/1` and `1/0`, the condition becoming articulate through a determination and the determination turning toward the condition it cannot make into another determinate possession, and held them together as `(0/1)/(1/0)`, the relation taking its own inverse as a term.[^s2-35] That expression is the whole of syn-ballein in notation. Each inner slash keeps the indefinite and the definite together, the outer slash relates the two readings of that keeping, and ordinary arithmetic, which defines `0/1` and leaves `1/0` undefined, supplies the seam through which the two readings stay different. A logic of this kind is complete in another sense than the classical one. It does not sort cases into boxes; it keeps the relation every sorting presupposes in view while the sorting goes on.

Syn-ballein is superpositional in the sense the dual-non-dual ontology of this essay gives the word. Ground and manifestation are distinguishable orientations of one appearing-act, each given through the relation that prevents it from standing alone, and separately complete substances related afterwards would already presuppose the joining they were meant to explain. Quantum state space, the complementary descriptions Pauli and Jung discussed, and the non-classical logics that allow a proposition to be both or neither are exact mathematical and physical neighbours of that claim, and §3 examines their agreements and differences in detail.[^s2-36] None of them supplies the claim. When we call `(0/1)/(1/0)` a superposition we mean that both orientations are present at once in the one relation and that the presence of each does not cancel the other, the way a mother's band and her baby's band are both fully readable at once and neither makes the other redundant.

Syn-ballein is not *the whole*. It is the logic of defining toward wholeness: the accounting in which a determination keeps its ground, its inverse orientation and the relations through which it can return, so that its completion stays a direction it travels in and never becomes a possession it holds. A claim to have achieved the whole would already be a `1` occupying the zero, which is what §0/1 · #2 called playing the `0`.[^s2-37] The retained seam keeps wholeness open. A token whose two halves had been fused into one lump would no longer be a token, and a gathering that claimed to have no remaining seams would be an enclosure, as §2 · #3 shows in the craftsman god's net.

Heraclitus gives the right kind of gathering a word, and Heidegger, reading him, gave the word a shape. In the fragment numbered B50, Heraclitus says that it is wise, listening not to him but to the *logos*, to agree that all things are one, and Heidegger, working back through *legein* to its oldest sense of laying down and gathering, rendered the Heraclitean Logos as "the Laying that gathers," *die lesende Lege*.[^s2-38] The gathering he heard in the word does not consume what it gathers. It lets what is gathered lie together before us, each thing where it is and as it is, as a harvester lays the gathered sheaves side by side, or as a reader, *legere*, gathers the letters of a line into a sentence without the letters ceasing to be letters. §0/1 · #4 recovered this root when it found the integral Logos to be a remembering of its own gathering.[^s2-39] A gathering that lets lie together before us is a fitting that keeps the pieces two, and its opposite, which §2 · #3 meets, is a gathering that holds together in order to arrest.

What a token carries across its interval is trust, and here syn-ballein shows its second face, the one it turns toward the uncertainty knowledge cannot eliminate. §2 · #0 said that knowledge is a performance of trust wearing the mask of certainty, and that the collapsed form of dia-ballein deals with the uncertainty it cannot admit by exporting it across the axis onto an excluded term.[^s2-40] Syn-ballein distributes it. Where the collapsed form finds one object to blame, syn-ballein finds many places to rest. A competence tested in use lets a carpenter trust her hands though she cannot prove they will not slip, a relationship that has survived disagreement gives a friend's word weight a stranger's would not carry, and a lineage, a practice, a piece of land, a ritual, a family, a source that has been checked before, an institution with real means of redress each give uncertainty somewhere to rest without pretending to abolish it. Each is a **provisional anchor**, provisional because it can be revised when it fails and an anchor because it holds while it holds. Their plurality is their strength. When one fails, as some will, the possibility of trusting does not fail with it, because the others go on bearing weight, and each can correct the others, so that an official account can be tested against practical knowledge and an intimate conviction against evidence it had refused to admit.

This is the trust I call mono–poly: one living field of reliance sustained through many anchors, none of which is permitted to stand for the whole. Its relation to the Mono and Poly of §0/1 · #1 is direct. Mono is the singular field, the reliance already enacted before anyone has certified it, which no anchor creates, and Poly is the many anchors through which that reliance becomes definite, local and revisable.[^s2-41] Sever the Poly and trust does not disappear; it becomes available for capture by a single totalising object, a leader, a doctrine, a party, a platform, a model, which offers to bear all the weight at once and asks in return to be exempt from the revision every anchor owes. That is the bargain the crowd of §2 · #1 accepted, and it is why the crowd's unity felt like relief. An isolated person with no anchors left has nowhere to rest their uncertainty except in the one place that offers to hold it all, and the monopoly of trust takes its name from the *pōlein*, to sell, that §0/1 · #4 traced in *monopoly*: one seller where there should be many.[^s2-42]

The vocabulary §0/1 opened when the household's reliance came under question can be followed through its whole course as six offices in the life of one entrustment.[^s2-43] *Fides*, the first, is reliance already enacted, the credit given to a witness before the witness has been weighed, the trust that comes before arbitration. A second office is *topos*, the place in which the relying happens: this source, these conditions, this person's competence and vulnerability, so that trust is never trust in general but always trust here. *Logos* is the third, the articulation of reasons and claims, the account that makes the reliance intelligible and open to examination. Then comes *nomos*, the instituted effect, which decides whose answer can change what is done and by which rule, through which office. *Natio*, from *nasci*, to be born, names the order into which later people arrive and begin living before they can examine how it was made, the belonging every generation inherits.[^s2-44] And *credere* is the renewed entrustment, credit extended again once an undertaking has returned its consequences, with what was learned carried into the new commitment. Read in order, the six describe how a single act of trust becomes a world: a reliance takes place somewhere, becomes an account, acquires the force of a rule, is inherited as a belonging and is renewed or withdrawn in the light of what happened. Read through the two logics, they show where trust can be captured. A *nomos* that forbids its own revision has arrested the sequence before *credere*, a *natio* that presents its order as nature has hidden the *topos* in which it was once made, and a *logos* that claims to need no *fides* has taken the mask for the face. Syn-ballein keeps the six offices moving, so that what was inherited can be examined and what was examined can be entrusted again.

The counter-operation to divide and conquer is **divine and concur**, a pun that argues. The phrase answers *divide and conquer* almost letter for letter, and the near-coincidence of the words carries the near-coincidence of the operations. To divide is to cut a field; to divine, Latin *dīvīnāre*, is to perceive what is hidden, the old art of the seer who reads in the visible signs a relation that does not itself appear.[^s2-45] Divining here means finding in the apparent self-sufficiency of each pole the relation it has obscured or appropriated: the transcendental third, the `0/1 = 1/0` relation through which both poles were formed and to which both still answer. The third so divined is not a third party standing in the middle of the axis, and not the centrist's midpoint, which remains on the signed line and merely chooses a location between `−1` and `+1`. It is the field that was divided so that these two terms now appear as mutually exclusive wholes, and the question that divines it is the one §2 · #1 left us with: who drew this line, who holds the combining step, and what do the two sides share that neither side's account of the other can see? The second half of the pun is sharper. *Conquer* descends, through Old French, from the Latin family of *conquīrere*, which Lewis and Short gloss as to seek for, to procure, and also to bring together and collect.[^s2-46] The conqueror, in the word's own history, gathers; he gathers by seizing, and the whole he assembles is held together by the hand that took it. *Concur* is *con-currere*, to run together, and its *currere* is the running we heard in *currency*, what is present enough to pass from hand to hand.[^s2-47] To concur is not to agree, still less to fuse or to settle at a midpoint. It is for differentiated positions to move together through a ground none of them possesses, as current money runs between people without belonging to any of them. Conquest gathers by possession and concurrence gathers by circulation.

Divine and concur can judge. A recovered relation does not make every pole equally factual, ethical, powerful or responsible, and recovering the field in which an injustice was done may sharpen the injustice: one claim may turn out to be false, a power may have to give up an office it had taken, and an injured person may decline reconciliation and be right to decline it. What the operation refuses is the step by which the falsity or violence of a determination licenses the fantasy that the people, histories and needs from which it arose can be expelled from the real. In practice it returns each institution, party and claim of authority to the people, labour, histories and material conditions it cannot own, and asks whose labour sustains the form, whose exclusion secures it, which office authorises it, which record makes it claimable, and by what path the governed may contest and alter it. It takes no view from nowhere and absolves no power. It is the practical condition under which a collective need not become a crowd in order to act together.

Computation has its own name for syn-ballein, and the name is the step the political trick withheld. In a divide-and-conquer algorithm the combine is where the subproblems' answers are brought back into the problem they were cut from, and in a larger computational process the same work is done by everything that lets a result carry its provenance. A result that keeps the problem it answered, the alternatives it excluded, the inverse reading that could contest it and the larger state it changed is a result that can return, and a result stripped of these is a number that can only be obeyed. §0/1 · #5→0 named the ontology in which this matters as Computational Process Ontology: process is ontologically prior to the finished thing, computation names the exact, repeatable side of that process, and epistemology is the process becoming able to state and inspect its own determinations.[^s2-48] Dia-ballein and syn-ballein are that ontology's primitive runtime. Dia makes the local branch actual: it distinguishes, compares, excludes, ranks, routes and decides. Syn keeps the branch's belonging to a wider field and composes its consequences with other branches: it relates, preserves provenance, inverts, recombines, contextualises and returns. A runtime of pure division atomises, and a runtime of pure gathering never decides anything at all.

*Agentworld* locates the intelligence of the coming agentic society in this composing step. "Long horizons are a property of groups," Bratton writes, and what lets a task run on indefinitely is "the composite's capacity to recompose itself around an evolving problem, passing coherence from sub-agent to artifact to sub-agent without meaningful loss."[^s2-49] And again: "The unit that learns is the ensemble, not the agent, and what it learns accrues to the commons between them, not to any single one."[^s2-50] Read through the two logics, these are claims about syn-ballein at planetary scale. The sub-agent is a cut, a local branch of a problem made tractable; the artifact passed between sub-agents is the token that carries the problem across the gap; and the coherence that passes without meaningful loss is the retained seam, the relation that lets each piece be read against the others. A commons into which learning accrues is a field of provisional anchors, and an ensemble that learns is mono–poly trust in technical form. The brief raises without answering the question this movement keeps asking: who holds the combining step? An ensemble whose recomposition is performed by every participant, with provenance visible to each, is concurrence. An ensemble whose recomposition is retained by one operator, while the sub-agents remain divided and their outputs pass upward through a channel only the operator can read, is divide and conquer with a better interface.

Return is an operation, and a file cannot perform it. A log can keep every step a system took, an audit trail can preserve every decision an institution made, and the archive can be complete while nothing it contains is able to change what happens next. Take a constructed case: a research agent whose reports carry, beside each claim, the retrieved page it rests on. A reviewer who opens one of those pages and finds that it does not say what the claim says has found a fault, and the fault can be handled in two ways. It can be recorded, in which case the report is corrected, the log keeps both versions, and the next run proceeds under the same rule for what counts as a source. Or it can reach the source, the criterion or the permission that let that page count as evidence, and change what the harness will accept as a citation from then on. Only the second is a return, because only there does the consequence arrive where the next act is decided. The maternity bands are read; they are not merely kept. A symbolon in a chest that nobody ever presents at the door proves nothing to anyone, and an account whose provenance is perfectly recorded and never consulted has kept the seam as a museum keeps a broken pot, intact and out of use.

The token has a modern counterfeit, and it shows what happens to trust when the seam itself can be manufactured. A photograph, a recording of a voice, a video of a public figure speaking: each has long worked as the half of a symbolon, a mark that could be carried away from the event that produced it and later presented as proof that the event took place, because its edge, the light that fell on the lens and the air that moved the microphone, fitted the event and nothing else. Synthetic media cut that fit. A generated image or voice presents itself as the half of a token whose other half never existed, and it fabricates the appearance of a relation to a source, a counterfeit symbolon. Its first harm is the obvious one, that people may believe what never happened. Its second is worse. Once a culture knows that the seam can be fabricated, a genuine record can be refused by claiming that it was fabricated too, and Robert Chesney and Danielle Citron named the advantage this gives to anyone caught on the record the liar's dividend.[^s2-51] The trust that lived in the fit of the halves has become available to both sides at once, so that no half can prove anything. Provenance systems, cryptographic signatures and content credentials can strengthen the conditions under which a sign returns to its source, and they are worth building, yet none of them manufactures trust from inside the mark. Somewhere a person or an institution still has to stand surety for the account, and who that is and what they risk by standing there is the question the myth of §2 · #3 puts at its centre.

Syn-ballein has a failure of its own. If dia-ballein's failure is severance, the cut that forgets its field, syn-ballein's is **fusion**: relation preserved only by erasing the distinctions through which its terms could meet. A fused relation has no seam left to read. The mother's band and the baby's band melted into one would match nothing; a marriage in which one partner's preferences have quietly become the other's has stopped being a relation between two people; a collective that speaks with one voice because every other voice has learned to keep quiet has achieved unity by abolishing the differences from which a reply could come. Fusion is harder to see than severance because it presents itself as love, or as consensus, or as the overcoming of division, and it can be welcomed by the very people it absorbs. Its test is the test of the token. Can the halves still be told apart? Can one of them still refuse, answer back, or leave? A relation in which that is no longer possible has stopped being a relation, and calling it whole does not change that.

Dia-ballein measures a real difference across a shared zero and collapses when it reads the zero as an ending, cancelling the difference or appropriating its span. Syn-ballein keeps the relation every measurement presupposes, holding the two orientations of a pair together, and collapses when it erases the difference that made the pair a pair. A life without the cut could not refuse and a life without the seam could not belong, and both fail in recognisable ways. What neither notation can show is what these operations feel like to the people performing them, what it is to be the one who separates, defends and refuses, or the one who attracts, joins and holds, and what happens when the two meet in a single bed. Greek myth gave that meeting a song, which §2 · #3 tells.

### M22 — Ares, Aphrodite and the Birth of Harmonia

A shipwrecked stranger sits at the table of a king who does not yet know his name. Earlier in the day the court's blind singer, Demodocus, sang of a quarrel between Odysseus and Achilles at Troy, and the stranger drew his purple cloak over his head and wept, and only the king noticed.[^s2-52] Then there were games on the shore, a running race and wrestling and the throwing of a discus, and a young man taunted the stranger, and the stranger threw a stone further than anyone had thrown before. Now the young men of the island clear a dancing floor, the herald brings Demodocus his lyre, and the dancers begin to strike the floor with their feet while the stranger watches the flashing of their steps and marvels. Demodocus sings a second song. It is about the gods, light and scandalous, told for pleasure to a hall that wants to be amused, and it gives the two logics the bodies §0/1 · #4 promised them, War and Love, Ares and Aphrodite, caught together in a net forged by the craftsman god.[^s2-53]

The song is short and complete, and it should be heard whole before anything is made of it. Ares has loved Aphrodite in secret, in the house of her husband Hephaestus, and has given her many gifts and shamed the husband's bed. Helios, the sun, who sees everything, has seen them lying together and goes to tell Hephaestus. The craftsman takes his grief to the forge. He sets his great anvil on its block and hammers out bonds that cannot be broken or loosed, fine as spiders' webs and invisible even to the gods, and he carries them to his chamber and hangs them all around the bedposts and from the rafters above. Then he pretends to leave for Lemnos, the island he loves best. Ares, who has been watching, sees him go, hurries to the house and takes Aphrodite by the hand: her husband is away, he says, among the barbarous Sintians, so let us go to bed. They lie down together, and the bonds fall on them, "and about them clung the cunning bonds of the wise Hephaestus, nor could they in any wise stir their limbs or raise them up. Then at length they learned that there was no more escaping."[^s2-54]

Helios has kept watch and goes back to Hephaestus, who turns round before he reaches Lemnos and comes home with his heart grieving. He stands in the doorway, savage anger seizes him, and he shouts to the gods: "Father Zeus, and ye other blessed gods that are forever, come hither that ye may see a laughable matter and a monstrous, even how Aphrodite, daughter of Zeus, scorns me for that I am lame and loves destructive Ares because he is comely and strong of limb, whereas I was born misshapen."[^s2-55] He will keep them there, he says, until her father has given back every one of the gifts he paid to win her. The gods come to the house of bronze, Poseidon the earth-shaker and Hermes and Apollo; "now the goddesses abode for shame each in her own house, but the gods, the givers of good things, stood in the gateway; and unquenchable laughter arose among the blessed gods as they saw the craft of wise Hephaestus."[^s2-56] One of them, glancing at his neighbour, draws the moral: bad deeds do not prosper, the slow catches the swift, and lame Hephaestus by his craft has caught Ares, the swiftest of all the gods on Olympus, so that Ares owes the fine of an adulterer. Then Apollo turns to Hermes and asks whether he would be willing to lie in such strong bonds beside golden Aphrodite, and Hermes answers that he would take three times as many bonds, with all the gods and all the goddesses looking on, to sleep beside her; and the gods laugh again.[^s2-57]

Only Poseidon does not laugh. He keeps begging Hephaestus to let Ares go, and he promises that Ares will pay whatever is right in the presence of the gods. Hephaestus refuses. A pledge given for a worthless man is a worthless pledge, he says in effect, and if Ares slips out of both the bonds and the debt, how could Hephaestus hold Poseidon to account among the immortals? Poseidon answers by changing what he offers. If Ares runs away and evades the debt, then Poseidon himself will pay it. And Hephaestus says that he cannot and must not refuse such a word, and he loosens the bonds. The two lovers spring up and are gone at once, Ares to Thrace and Aphrodite, laughter-loving, to Cyprus, to Paphos, where she has her precinct and her fragrant altar, and there the Graces bathe her and anoint her with immortal oil and dress her in lovely clothes. That is the end of the song, and the stranger is glad at heart as he listens, and so are the Phaeacians, long-oared men, famed for their ships.[^s2-58]

The song is a story about two powers and a third. Ares is war: the god of the line that holds, the shield and the spear, contest and refusal and the force by which a difference can stand its ground and say no. Aphrodite is love: attraction and pleasure and the movement of joining, the power that draws a life out of isolation and makes an encounter worth risking something for. They are the two logics given bodies, and the bodies show what the notation could not, what each operation is like from inside and why each needs the other. Ares without Aphrodite is difference that has forgotten relation: every other becomes an enemy, every boundary a front line, and the capacity to refuse, which is a real good, hardens into the capacity only to refuse. Aphrodite without Ares is relation that has forgotten difference: joining becomes engulfing, attraction becomes possession, and the meeting of two lives becomes the disappearance of one into the other. Each gives the other what it lacks. Ares gives Aphrodite beings distinct enough to meet, since only what can stand apart can come together, and a lover who could not refuse would have nothing to give. Aphrodite gives Ares a reason for his defences, since a boundary that protects nothing has no purpose, and the line holds because something on its far side is loved. I read the song as an argued mytheme, a whole image that proves a relation through the action it stages, and I read it back into operations without making Homer the author of our logics.[^s2-59]

§0/1 · #2 put the question this pairing answers in its plainest form: will difference become a dance, or a battle?[^s2-60] The dancers on the Phaeacian floor, striking the ground in time while Demodocus sings, are a working answer. A dance is a difference kept in motion: two or twenty bodies, each distinct, each moving through a shared space by rules that keep them from colliding and keep them related, so that the pattern of the whole depends on every dancer staying a dancer. A battle is a difference that has demanded a winner. Opposition, contest, criticism and even fierce disagreement can remain inside a held polarity, `(−1)/(+1)`, where the zero still connects the poles and each still has its sense through the other, and that is the line between the two logics' healthy and collapsed forms. War is the demand that the slash produce a winner, the moment at which the other ceases to be a pole with whom a world is shared and becomes an obstacle whose removal is imagined to complete the world.[^s2-61] Ares at his worst is that demand made into a god. Aphrodite at her worst is its mirror, the demand that the slash produce one body, that the other's difference be dissolved into the lover's desire. Both demands refuse the slash.

Jung saw the psychological shape of this pairing, and saw it with an exactness that bears directly on the myth. In the first of his *Two Essays on Analytical Psychology*, comparing Freud's psychology of Eros with Adler's psychology of power, he observed that life can flow forward only along a gradient, and that "there is no energy unless there is a tension of opposites." Then he named the opposite of love: "Logically, the opposite of love is hate, and of Eros, Phobos (fear); but psychologically it is the will to power. Where love reigns, there is no will to power; and where the will to power is paramount, love is lacking. The one is but the shadow of the other."[^s2-62] Earlier in the essay he had quoted Freud's late formulation of the two basic instincts, Eros, whose aim is "to establish ever greater unities and to preserve them thus—in short, to bind together," and the destructive instinct, whose aim is "to undo connections and so to destroy things."[^s2-63] Freud's pair and Jung's pair are not our pair, and each belongs to its own argument. But each describes, in its own register, the two directions of the throw, binding together and undoing connections, syn-ballein and dia-ballein, and each insists, as the myth does, that the two belong to one energy. Jung's sentence about Phobos has a further edge. In Hesiod's *Theogony* the logical opposite of love is literally one of love's children.

"Also Cytherea bare to Ares the shield-piercer Panic and Fear, terrible gods who drive in disorder the close ranks of men in numbing war, with the help of Ares, sacker of towns; and Harmonia whom high-spirited Cadmus made his wife."[^s2-64] Hesiod gives the union of War and Love three children, and two of them are terrors. Deimos and Phobos, Panic and Fear, ride with their father into battle and break the ranks of men, while Harmonia marries the founder of Thebes and becomes the mother of a royal house. A meeting of the power that separates and the power that joins can bear fear or it can bear harmony, and Hesiod sets both outcomes in one genealogy, so that neither can be taken as the meeting's guaranteed result. Read through the two logics, the difference between the children is the difference between the collapsed and the held polarity. Where the meeting of War and Love demands a winner, its offspring is fear: the lover becomes a threat, the beloved a possession to be guarded, and the energy Jung found in the tension of opposites becomes panic, the rout of ranks that no longer know what holds them together. Where the meeting holds its tension without settling it, its offspring is harmony. Harmonia is born of War and Love together, and only where neither parent has swallowed the other.

Her name says how. Greek *harmonia* began as a word of craft: in the *Odyssey*, when Odysseus builds his raft on Calypso's island, he fastens its timbers together with pegs and *harmoniai*, joints, the fittings by which separate pieces of wood are made to hold as one vessel.[^s2-65] From the joint of a carpenter the word passed to an agreement between people: in the *Iliad*, before their last fight, Hector asks Achilles to swear that the victor will give back the loser's body, and calls on the gods as the best witnesses and guardians of *harmoniai*, compacts.[^s2-66] And from the joint and the compact it passed to music, the fitting of sounds into an ordered relation, which is the sense the word has carried ever since. A joint, a covenant, an attunement: craft, trust and music, three senses of one word, and they are the three things this myth is about. Hephaestus's net is a terrible joint, a fitting that holds two bodies together and lets neither move. Poseidon's surety is a covenant, a word given before witnesses. The bow and the lyre, which Heraclitus set side by side, are the attunement that holds tension without breaking it. Achilles' answer to Hector shows what happens when the second sense is refused. There are no faithful oaths between lions and men, he says, nor do wolves and lambs have one heart; there can be no compact between you and me.[^s2-67] That is dia-ballein absolutised, war as the demand that the slash produce a winner, spoken by the greatest warrior of the poem, and its consequence is the dragging of Hector's body around the walls of Troy.

Heraclitus gave *harmonia* its philosophical form in a single sentence. "They do not understand how in differing it agrees with itself; a backwards-turning fastening, just as that of a bow or a lyre."[^s2-68] The word Mackenzie translates as *fastening* is *harmoniē*, the same word, and the sentence says in its own terms what Hesiod's genealogy staged: a joining that holds through a pull in two directions. Bend a bow and its two arms pull against the string while the string pulls against them, and the tension of the whole is what lets it send an arrow; string a lyre and the frame pulls against the strings while the strings pull against the frame, and the tension is what lets it sound. Removing the tension would not perfect the agreement of bow and string; it would abolish the bow. The verb for *agrees* is *homologeei*, and §2 · #0 heard that *homologia* is a common *logos* found within a difference.[^s2-69] Heraclitus's agreement is an agreement made of the parts' differing, and the parts never stop differing. Bow-arms do not have to be reconciled before the bow can work. Their opposition, held, is the work.

Mackenzie argues that the fragment alludes to the *Odyssey*, and to a scene in which the same stranger who listened to Demodocus's song takes up a bow.[^s2-70] At the end of the poem, home at last in Ithaca, disguised as a beggar in his own hall among the suitors who have been devouring his house, Odysseus is handed the great bow that none of them has been able to string. He strings it without effort, the way a man skilled in the lyre and in song stretches a string around a new peg, and he plucks the string with his right hand, and it sings beautifully, like the voice of a swallow.[^s2-71] The bow becomes a lyre in his hands for a moment before it becomes a bow again, and then it kills. Homer supplies the image, and the allusion is Mackenzie's argument; the reading is ours. The man who heard the song of the net is the man who will hold together, in one instrument, the two powers the song set against each other, the tension of war and the tension of music, and his homecoming depends on his knowing that they are the same tension differently released.

*Hamartia*, which §0/1 · #2 traced to its root in missing the mark, finds its image here.[^s2-72] The word was first said of a spear thrown and falling short of its target, and §0/1 located the error it names where a mark is required to stand as though it had abolished its difference from what it marks. The bow gives that error a body. An archer who has forgotten that the bow is also a lyre treats the tension of the instrument as nothing but the means of reaching the target, and the target as the whole meaning of the act. He can hit what he aimed at and still miss, because the mark he struck was never the whole of what the act concerned: the condition that made it a mark, the relation in which the shot was taken and the life the arrow enters, has dropped out of the aiming. The bow forgets it is a lyre when tension is collapsed into a target. An achieved aim can miss its own ground in this way, and a technical success can be a *hamartia*: the arrow lands where it was sent, and nothing in the landing asks whether it should have been sent there.

Hephaestus is the third figure, and the song is careful about what kind of power he has. He is lame, the only Olympian with a damaged body, born misshapen as he complains to the gods, and he wins, against the swiftest of the gods, by craft. Homer's word for the bonds that pour around the lovers is *desmoi technēentes*, which Murray renders "cunning bonds" and which says, literally, bonds full of *technē*: craft is written on the net itself.[^s2-73] The gods' moral, that the slow catches the swift, names the reversal by which a weaker power defeats a stronger one through cleverness, and Marcel Detienne and Jean-Pierre Vernant made that reversal the signature of a whole Greek category of intelligence, *mētis*, cunning craft, at home in shifting and ambiguous situations, whose characteristic instruments are the trap, the net, the woven circle and the bond. For them Hephaestus's crooked feet are themselves the visible sign of this intelligence, a body that walks two ways at once, suited to mastering what is fluid and slippery.[^s2-74] The net is *mētis* made into an object, finer than spider silk, invisible, closing around the bed so that no movement in any direction can escape it.

Every station of a modern apparatus is already present in what the net does, step by step. Detection comes first: Helios sees, and the poem gives him a lookout from which he keeps watch for Hephaestus and reports twice, once to set the trap and once to spring it.[^s2-75] Fabrication follows, the bonds forged in secret, invisible to those they will hold. Concealment makes them effective, the pretended journey to Lemnos inviting the lovers into a room already prepared. Capture holds them: they cannot stir a limb, and only then do they learn there is no escape. Display turns capture into evidence, because Hephaestus summons the gods to come and *see* and the scene's whole purpose becomes the making of a public sight. A tribunal forms in the gateway, its verdict pronounced by an anonymous god. An account converts grievance into debt: Hephaestus demands back the bride-gifts, *hedna*, he paid for his wife, and the onlookers name the fine the captured adulterer owes, *moichagria*, a word Greek uses only here.[^s2-76] And an economy of exposure appears, spoken aloud by Hermes, who would accept three times the bonds and every god and goddess looking on for the pleasure of the bed. Christopher Brown has shown that Greek communities really did expose adulterers to public mockery, and that the Olympian scene is shaped by that social practice; the laughter is the punishment.[^s2-77] The shame falls unevenly. The goddesses stay at home, and the gods stand in the gateway and enjoy what the exposed goddess is being held responsible for.

Martin Heidegger's account of the essence of modern technology gives this sequence a name that can carry weight, though Heidegger never read the song this way and the reading is ours. Modern technology, he argued, reveals the world as *Bestand*, standing-reserve: "Everywhere everything is ordered to stand by, to be immediately at hand, indeed to stand there just so that it may be on call for a further ordering."[^s2-78] The lovers under the net are standing-reserve, held where they are, at hand, on view, waiting for an ordering that is not theirs. Heidegger called the way of revealing that orders the world into standing-reserve *Ge-stell*, enframing, and derived the word from the gathering force of the German prefix *Ge-*, as in *Gebirg*, the gathering of mountains into a range, and *Gemüt*, the gathering of feelings into a disposition: "We now name that challenging claim which gathers man thither to order the self-revealing as standing-reserve: 'Ge-stell' [Enframing]." Enframing, he said, "means the gathering together of that setting-upon which sets upon man."[^s2-79] *Ge-stell* is a gathering, a word shaped like syn-ballein for an operation that works like dia-ballein. Hephaestus's net shows the paradox in one image. It throws the lovers together, literally, a syn-ballein in the most kinetic sense, and it is exactly by throwing them together that it arrests them. The essay's name for this is the **counterfeit gathering**: a gathering that keeps the differences visible and keeps the relation visible and arrests the reciprocity between them, so that the gathered can neither move nor answer back. Fusion removes difference and severance removes relation, whereas the counterfeit gathering keeps both on display and makes both inert.[^s2-80]

Homer's own word for the device is *dolos*, a snare, and the verb *diaballein* does not appear in the scene. What Hephaestus enacts before the convened gods is nonetheless *diabolē* in the sense the lexicon keeps: an accusation staged as public exposure, parties set at variance before witnesses, a charge thrown across between two people so that one appears to all the others under its terms.[^s2-81] Naming it so is our move, and it gives dia-ballein a mythic body exactly where syn-ballein has always had one. A symbolon is a token whose two halves fit across a seam, and the net is a device whose two captives are held together across no seam at all, with the captor, the protocol and the audience standing where the zero should be. In the notation the lovers have become exposed terms, `−1` and `+1` displayed side by side, and the axis between them, the relation through which each had its sense, has been occupied by the apparatus. Hephaestus stands in the place of the shared zero and counts the whole span from his own end: his grievance, his gifts, his fine. The span can be counted from either end. Counted from his, as it is, the span is `(+1)−(−1)=+2`, his grievance made the measure of the scene; the same span is what the lovers carry as `(−1)−(+1)=−2`, the exposure and the fine they bear for his loss.

The apparatus, complete at every station, cannot conclude. Detection has succeeded, the bonds have held, the evidence is before every eye and the verdict has been spoken, and the scene stalls. The lovers remain bound, the grievance remains open, and the demand for the bride-gifts has no mechanism inside the net for being met, because a trap can hold a debtor and cannot make a debt good. If Hephaestus keeps them there forever he has a captive and no payment, and if he lets them go he has no guarantee. Everything a net can do has been done, and what the situation now needs is something the net cannot make: a relation in which someone undertakes, at his own risk, to answer for what happens after the bonds are opened. Poseidon supplies it, in two steps. His first offer is a promise about another's conduct, that Ares "shall himself pay thee all that is right in the presence of the immortal gods," and Hephaestus refuses it with a craftsman's distrust: "A sorry thing to be sure of is the surety for a sorry knave." His second offer differs in kind. Poseidon makes the possible failure his own: "even if Ares shall avoid the debt and flee away, I will myself pay thee this." Greek has a word for this undertaking, *engyē*, the pledge or surety placed in another's hand, and the song stages it with the precision of a legal procedure.[^s2-82] Hephaestus accepts, against his own stated distrust, because nothing else can open the bonds and close the account, and he uses the same hands that made the net to unmake it.

That is the turn the myth makes without a single abstract word. An apparatus that replaced an encounter with a capture is returned, at its own limit, to trust. A person standing for another at real risk of loss, a relation no mechanism generated, is what the mechanism's own maker has to borrow in order to finish what his craft began. *Agentworld* offers a definition of trust for its society of agents that the scene tests directly. "Trust here," Bratton writes, "is not a moral category but a prediction-stability category: an agent is trusted to the degree its behavior remains well-modeled across the adversarial and cooperative transitions that punctuate any long interaction."[^s2-83] Under the net the lovers are perfectly modelled. Their behaviour is entirely predictable, since they can do nothing, and their legibility is total, so that trust in Bratton's sense is at its maximum at the very moment the relation is most stuck. What releases them is a different category, which the brief's scoped definition does not need to deny but cannot contain: a personed liability, an undertaking whose bearer stands to lose something if the prediction fails. Bratton goes on to say that stability is "not the absence of conflict but the calibration of mutual — if variously symmetric and asymmetric — legibility and illegibility," and the net is the abolition of illegibility.[^s2-84] Total legibility arrests the captive and the captor together and leaves them both waiting for a pledge. The scene returns twice. In §5 · #1 it becomes a technical claim about preference learning, that a finished score hides whoever stands surety for it, and in §5→0 · #3 it becomes a design test: a system can represent both sides of a conflict, keep an immaculate audit trail and meet every benchmark, and remain Hephaestian if its representation has become a substitute for the relation it claims to secure.[^s2-85] Technical synthesis becomes syn-ballein when the governed parties keep their agency, their provenance, their power to contest and their route of return, and reciprocal legibility stops short of total capture.

Another net lies in the record of human imagination, spun to show the opposite operation. §0 · #3 told the Huayan jewel net of Indra in full: a jewel at every knot, each reflecting all the others, so that one jewel marked in the southwest shows its ink dot everywhere in the ten directions. Set beside Hephaestus's net, it shows the two technical destinies of every web.[^s2-indra] Indra's net figures `0/1`, each jewel definite, selectable and markable, and each the place through which the whole field becomes present, so that relation is active inside every determination. Hephaestus's net figures the polarity arrested, two bodies exposed as terms, their relation occupied by the captor, the protocol and the audience. We live inside a net of the first kind's ambition built, often, to the second kind's design, a world-wide web in which every node can in principle reflect every other and in which, increasingly, every node is watched, held, displayed and priced. What both nets ask of that web is what the song put to the gods in the gateway: does the gathering preserve the relation through which the gathered can answer, or does it make their relation into evidence and their difference into a spectacle?

Eros has been present throughout the song without being named. Hesiod places him at the beginning of the world, among the first powers to come into being after Chaos and Earth, the one who loosens limbs and overpowers the mind of gods and men; and when Aphrodite rises from the sea, Eros and Himeros, Desire, attend her coming among the gods.[^s2-89] He is the desiring-between, the force that makes a relation more than the coexistence of two separate things, and in the song he is the reason the lovers met at all and the reason Hermes would accept three times the bonds. §0/1 · #3 named the participation of desire in knowing the eros of Logos, and gave Jung's pairing its place: Logos as discrimination, judgment and insight, Eros as the capacity to relate.[^s2-90] The myth lays out the same structure in persons. Ares is the discriminating force, the line that holds and refuses; Aphrodite is the relating force, the movement that joins; Eros is the desire that runs between them and makes their meeting generative; and Harmonia is what their meeting produces when neither swallows the other, the fitting of the cut and the joining into one form that keeps both. The eros of Logos is the desire of articulation to recover the relations its own discriminations reveal, and Harmonia is that desire satisfied without being exhausted, a joint that holds because both its pieces still pull.

Demodocus's song ends in no harmony. Homer gives the lovers no child and the marriage no repair. Ares goes to Thrace and Aphrodite to Paphos, and the Graces bathe her and dress her; the debt's payment is never narrated, and whether Poseidon ever had to make good his word the poem does not say. Harmonia's birth belongs to Hesiod, not to Homer, and the contrast between the two tellings is ours to draw: the marriage of craft that bound Aphrodite to Hephaestus bears no Harmonia, and her union with War, in another poem, does. What the song does show, completely, is the passage from capture to entrustment. The bonds have been undone by the hands that made them, the grievance remains a grievance, a god has made himself answerable for what happens next, and the lovers have paths beyond the image in which they were held. Released, the relation goes on into a future the apparatus does not contain.

And the stranger listens, and is glad. In a few hours he will tell the Phaeacians his name, and in a few days they will carry him home asleep in one of their swift ships, and in his own hall he will string a bow like a lyre. Whether he heard in the song anything about his own homecoming the poem does not tell us. What a mytheme can do this one has done, in an action no one could mistake: the joint, the covenant and the attunement are, in Greek, one word.
