[^s01-m03-s01-derrida]: Jacques Derrida, “Différance,” in *Margins of Philosophy*, trans. Alan Bass (University of Chicago Press, 1982), 3–5 (the silent *a*), 8 (the two senses of *différer*) and 11 (no concept present in itself; every concept inscribed in a chain or system of differences), within 1–27.

[^s01-m03-s01-lacan-glissement]: Jacques Lacan, “The Instance of the Letter in the Unconscious, or Reason since Freud” (1957), in *Écrits: The First Complete Edition in English*, trans. Bruce Fink (W. W. Norton, 2006), 418–19 (the sliding of the signified under the signifier, held at a few anchoring points) and 419 (signification insists in the chain, not in any one element of it). On the *point de capiton*, see Jacques Lacan, *The Psychoses, 1955–1956*, ed. Jacques-Alain Miller, trans. Russell Grigg, The Seminar of Jacques Lacan, bk. 3 (W. W. Norton, 1993), chap. 21, “The Quilting Point.” The comparison with the sliding of the Subject in the definition is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-redbook]: Jung, *Red Book*, 242 (Liber Primus, chap. 7, “Murder of the Hero”).

[^s01-m03-s01-heraclitus]: Heraclitus, frags. B12 and B91, numbered as in Hermann Diels and Walther Kranz, *Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker*, 6th ed. (Weidmann, 1951–52); compare Plato, *Cratylus* 402a (DK 22 A6), trans. Harold N. Fowler (Harvard University Press, 1921). English renderings of the fragments are from Daniel W. Graham, “Heraclitus,” *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*, rev. December 8, 2023, §3.1: B12, “On those stepping into rivers staying the same other and other waters flow”; B91 (from Plutarch), “It is not possible to step twice into the same river,” which Graham treats as a paraphrase of B12. Where Heraclitus speaks of stepping into the same river, the essay’s sentence says “crossed.”

[^s01-m03-s01-mata]: *Mata v. Avianca, Inc.*, 678 F. Supp. 3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023) (No. 22-cv-1461 (PKC), opinion and order on sanctions, June 22, 2023, ECF No. 54), slip op. at 7–9, 15–17 (Findings of Fact ¶¶ 13–14, 18, 22, 36, 38–40). The filing was an affirmation in opposition to a motion to dismiss; the court’s orders of April 11 and 12 required copies of the cited decisions; the April 25 affidavit annexed excerpts only; the respondents acknowledged that the decisions were generated by ChatGPT, and the court found that Schwartz had no full text of any of them and quoted only from chatbot excerpts. The inference in the sentence that follows is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-diaballein]: Henry George Liddell and Robert Scott, *A Greek-English Lexicon*, rev. Henry Stuart Jones with Roderick McKenzie, 9th ed. (Clarendon Press, 1940), s.vv. “συμβάλλω” (“throw together,” “bring together”), “διαβάλλω” (“throw or carry over or across”; “set at variance”; “attack a man’s character, calumniate”; also “accuse”) and “διάβολος” (“slanderer”; “enemy,” Septuagint Esther 7.4, 8.1; “Satan,” 1 Chronicles 21.1 in the Septuagint; “the Devil,” Matthew 4.1). “Throwing apart” is not a gloss the lexicon gives; it is the author’s reading of the prefix.

[^s01-m03-s01-spencerbrown]: G. Spencer-Brown, *Laws of Form* (Allen & Unwin, 1969), chap. 11, “Equations of the second degree,” 57–58, where an expression that re-enters itself is given an imaginary state, a state of time rather than of space. Reading the hardened opposition as this alternation arrested is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-monocultures]: The analysis of the two monocultures is the author’s. Its application to party politics illustrates the structure and makes no empirical claim about any particular electorate.

[^s01-m03-s01-lacan-nof]: Jacques Lacan, “On a Question Prior to Any Possible Treatment of Psychosis” (1957–58), in Lacan, *Écrits*, 445–88; and Lacan, *Psychoses*. The account of the parent as administering an order that binds them to obligations toward the child is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-wolin]: Sheldon S. Wolin, *Democracy Incorporated: Managed Democracy and the Specter of Inverted Totalitarianism* (Princeton University Press, 2008), chap. 3 (“Totalitarianism’s Inversion, Democracy’s Perversion”), chap. 8 (“The Politics of Superpower: Managed Democracy”) and chap. 11 (“Inverted Totalitarianism: Antecedents and Precedents”). The representative as the face of that power, and the reading of the representative as scapegoat that follows, with its two collapses, are the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-john]: John 12:31 (see also 14:30, 16:11), “the prince of this world”; 18:36; on the Comforter (Greek *paraklētos*), 14:16, 26; compare 17:21 (King James Version, eBible `eng-kjv2006`, standardized 1769 text). The reading of Father, Son and Spirit through `0/1` is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-hamartia]: Liddell and Scott, *Greek-English Lexicon*, s.vv. “ἁμαρτία” (“a failure, fault”; “error of judgement,” Thucydides 1.32; in philosophy and religion “guilt, sin,” Plato, *Laws* 660c; Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* 1148a3; Septuagint Genesis 18.20; John 8.46) and “ἁμαρτάνω” (“miss the mark,” first of a thrown spear, *Iliad* 5.287, then “do wrong, err, sin”). The sense “miss the mark” belongs first to the verb. The reading of the missed mark through the symbolon is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-native]: The definition is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-theodicy]: G. W. Leibniz, *Essais de Théodicée sur la bonté de Dieu, la liberté de l’homme et l’origine du mal* (Amsterdam: Isaac Troyel, 1710); in English, *Theodicy: Essays on the Goodness of God, the Freedom of Man, and the Origin of Evil*, trans. E. M. Huggard, ed. Austin Farrer (Open Court, 1985). Leibniz formed the word from *theos*, god, and *dikē*, justice, and had used it in French and Latin forms in the mid-1690s; see Thomas Feeney, “Leibniz on the Problem of Evil,” *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*, first published January 12, 2026.

[^s01-m03-s01-omni]: The completion of the four classical predicates by omnivalence and omni-lemmicity is the author’s. On *lēmma*, from *lambanein*, see Liddell and Scott, *Greek-English Lexicon*, s.v. “λῆμμα”: “anything received,” and in logic a “statement taken as true,” an assumption, especially a premiss (Aristotle, *Topics* 101a14, 156a21).

[^s01-m03-s01-nirguna]: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6 (“No, no!” in Max Müller’s rendering, not “not this, not this”); see also 3.9.26, 4.2.4, 4.4.22, 4.5.15, in *The Upanishads, Part II*, trans. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East 15 (Clarendon Press, 1884), 108. For Eckhart’s distinction between God and Godhead, see his German sermon 52, “Beati pauperes spiritu” (Josef Quint’s number), in *The Complete Mystical Works of Meister Eckhart*, trans. and ed. Maurice O’C. Walshe, rev. Bernard McGinn (Crossroad, 2009).

[^s01-m03-s01-exodus]: Exod. 3:12, 14 (JPS 1917, in the Mechon Mamre Hebrew–English text): “Certainly I will be with thee”; “I AM THAT I AM.” The Hebrew *ehyeh asher ehyeh* also admits the rendering “I will be what I will be”: the note to Exod. 3:14 in the 1985 JPS *Tanakh* calls the meaning of the Hebrew uncertain and lists “I Am That I Am,” “I Am Who I Am” and “I Will Be What I Will Be” among the renderings.

[^s01-m03-s01-aion-shadow]: C. G. Jung, *Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self*, 2nd ed., trans. R. F. C. Hull, Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 9, pt. 2 (Princeton University Press, 1979), ¶14 for the first two quoted phrases (the shadow as a moral problem; recognizing its dark aspects as present and real) and ¶16 for the third (projection placing the cause of the emotion in the other person).

[^s01-m03-s01-kelo]: *Kelo v. City of New London*, 545 U.S. 469 (2005). Facts: 472–75 (the New London Development Corporation, “a private nonprofit entity,” 473; Pfizer’s adjacent research facility, 473; the plan’s hotel, about 80 residences and office parcels, 474; the city council’s approval in January 2000 and its authorisation of the corporation to acquire property by eminent domain in the city’s name, 475). Holding: the plan serves a “public use,” 483–84 and 489–90. Justice Stevens wrote for the Court, joined by Justices Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; Justice O’Connor dissented, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices Scalia and Thomas, *id.* at 494; Justice Thomas also dissented, *id.* at 505.

[^s01-m03-s01-pfizer]: Patrick McGeehan, “Pfizer to Leave City That Won Land-Use Case,” *New York Times*, November 12, 2009, https://www.nytimes.com/2009/11/13/nyregion/13pfizer.html (print headline “… Land-Use Suit,” New York edition, p. A1). Pfizer announced on Monday, November 9, that it would leave New London; the article describes the cleared land on which the planned hotel, stores and condominiums were never built. For the long vacancy: JC Sevcik, “9 Years after SCOTUS’ *Kelo* Ruling, Houses Seized under Eminent Domain Remain Undeveloped,” UPI, March 20, 2014; John Penney, “Construction of 500 Apartments at Fort Trumbull Still a Go,” *The Day* (New London, CT), July 17, 2024 (parcels vacant for almost twenty years). The text states both facts generally and claims no figures.

[^s01-m03-s01-slapp]: George W. Pring and Penelope Canan, *SLAPPs: Getting Sued for Speaking Out* (Temple University Press, 1996), chap. 1 (definition and process). Pring and Canan coined the term; their earlier article is Penelope Canan and George W. Pring, “Strategic Lawsuits against Public Participation,” *Social Problems* 35, no. 5 (1988): 506–19, https://doi.org/10.1525/sp.1988.35.5.03a00030. For reputation-management firms and wealthy claimants, see, for example, United Kingdom, Ministry of Justice, *Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation (SLAPPs): A Call for Evidence* (2022), 3, 5. The compression of the suit’s aim as burdening critics more than winning is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-carlin]: George Carlin, *Life Is Worth Losing*, directed by Rocco Urbisci (HBO, broadcast live November 5, 2005, from the Beacon Theatre, New York), in the closing routine on “the real owners” of the country, shortly before the “American dream” line. The locator is the routine; the wording is checked against an unofficial transcript only. The reading of the line as syn-ballein for members and dia-ballein for outsiders is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-dialog]: Dell Cameron and Yulia Almazova, “Leak Exposes Members of Peter Thiel’s Secretive ‘Dialog’ Society,” *Wired*, June 16, 2026, https://www.wired.com/story/leak-exposes-members-of-peter-thiels-secretive-dialog-society/; Dell Cameron, Dhruv Mehrotra, and Yulia Almazova, “How the Peter Thiel-Linked Dialog Club Secretly Ranks Its Members,” *Wired*, June 18, 2026, https://www.wired.com/story/how-peter-thiels-private-dialog-club-secretly-ranks-its-members/. The first article reports a website directory of 113 names (independently verified by *Wired*; it lists two US senators and sitting administration officials, among them the Treasury secretary) and a separate registration list for the August 2026 retreat naming 222 people (it lists a NATO commander among others); the second gives the 2006 founding by Thiel and Auren Hoffman and reports the grades by wealth and fame, the relationship tracking and the algorithmic matching of whom attendees meet and sit with. *Wired* itself says the registration records “appear to show” who attends, and the retreat had not yet taken place; inclusion in the directory or the registration records, active membership and attendance are different things, so the text names offices and sectors and calls no individual a member. The reading of the leak as a topology is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-epstein-redaction]: Epstein Files Transparency Act, Pub. L. No. 119-38, § 2(b)(1), (c), 139 Stat. 656, 657 (2025) (no record to be redacted “on the basis of embarrassment, reputational harm, or political sensitivity”); Todd Blanche to Members of Congress, December 19, 2025, letter on the production of the Epstein files, U.S. Department of Justice, 1–4, https://www.justice.gov/opa/media/1434851/dl (six pages). The letter gives the Review Protocol’s five grounds of redaction and a “limited amount” of privileged withholding (2) and the victim-name redactions and the numbering of the released records (3); it does not quantify the redactions. On their extent: CBS News counted at least 550 pages entirely redacted in the first release (Joe Walsh, “Over 500 Pages in Initial Epstein Files Release Were Entirely Blacked Out, CBS News Finds,” *CBS News*, December 20, 2025, updated December 21, 2025, https://www.cbsnews.com/texas/news/epstein-files-redaction-over-500-pages-entirely-blacked-out); the Department reported about 3.5 million pages published by January 30, 2026 and gave no count of redactions (U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, “Department of Justice Publishes 3.5 Million Responsive Pages in Compliance with the Epstein Files Transparency Act,” press release, January 30, 2026, https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/department-justice-publishes-35-million-responsive-pages-compliance-epstein-files); and Representatives Massie and Khanna, having viewed the unredacted files, said the names of six men had been redacted, which the Department answered by pointing to legal requirements (Yashraj Sharma, “Six Men Named in US Congress: Why Is So Much Redacted in the Epstein Files?,” *Al Jazeera*, February 11, 2026, https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/2/11/six-men-named-in-us-congress-why-is-so-much-redacted-in-the-epstein-files). The record shows extensive and contested redaction, not total redaction; the characterisation of it as an instance of obfuscation is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-snowden-assange]: Edward Snowden: criminal complaint filed in the Eastern District of Virginia and made public on June 21, 2013, charging theft of government property and Espionage Act offences (Will Dunham, “Federal Prosecutors Charge Edward Snowden over NSA Leaks,” Reuters, June 21, 2013, reproduced in *Christian Science Monitor*, https://www.csmonitor.com/layout/set/amphtml/USA/2013/0621/Federal-prosecutors-charge-Edward-Snowden-over-NSA-leaks); temporary asylum in Russia from August 1, 2013 (“Snowden Leaves Moscow Airport,” *Al Jazeera*, August 1, 2013, https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2013/8/1/snowden-leaves-moscow-airport); he has lived in Russia since. Julian Assange: arrested in London on April 11, 2019 on a US extradition request; an eighteen-count superseding indictment in the Eastern District of Virginia, seventeen counts under the Espionage Act provisions of 18 U.S.C. § 793, was filed May 23, 2019 (Superseding Indictment, *United States v. Assange*, No. 1:18-cr-00111-CMH, ECF No. 31 (E.D. Va. filed May 23, 2019), 1, https://www.justice.gov/d9/press-releases/attachments/2019/05/23/assange_superseding_indictment_1.pdf); held in Belmarsh Prison from about April 11, 2019 pending extradition, about sixty-two months, until the plea agreement of June 2024, under which he pleaded guilty in the Northern Mariana Islands to one count of conspiracy to obtain and disclose national defense information, was sentenced to time served and returned to Australia (Plea Agreement, *United States v. Assange*, No. CR 24-00014 (D.N. Mar. I. June 2024), 12, https://justice.gov/opa/media/1358636/dl). The comparison of the two cases is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-digit]: Lewis and Short, *Latin Dictionary*, s.vv. “digitus” (“a finger”; *computare digitis*, “to count on the fingers”) and “manipulus” (“a handful, a bundle,” formed from *manus* and the root of *plenus*). Harper, *Online Etymology Dictionary*, s.v. “digit,” dates *digit* as a numeral below ten to the late fourteenth century, numerals under ten having been counted on the fingers. *Manipulation*, attested by 1730 of a method of digging ore, reached English through French; *The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language*, 5th ed., s.v. “manipulation,” adds a Spanish stage, and Harper, s.v. “manipulation,” gives French *manipule*, “handful,” a pharmacists’ measure.

[^s01-m03-s01-nietzsche-market]: Friedrich Nietzsche, *The Gay Science: With a Prelude in Rhymes and an Appendix of Songs*, trans. Walter Kaufmann (New York: Vintage Books, 1974), §125 (“The Madman”), 181–82. In the parable the madman lights a lantern in the morning and runs to the marketplace (*Markt*) to announce that God is dead. The reading of why the news belongs there is the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-trust]: The distinctions among trust, knowledge, belief and faith, and the account of faith as lucid continuation through the limit, are the author’s.

[^s01-m03-s01-fides]: Lewis and Short, *Latin Dictionary*, s.v. “fides”: “trust in a person or thing, faith, confidence, reliance, credence, belief,” with the sense of credibility illustrated from Cicero, *De officiis* 2.9.33 (“to give confidence”), and *Pro Sulla* 3.10 (testimony); the entry derives *fides* from *fido*.

[^s01-m03-s01-arbiter]: Lewis and Short, *Latin Dictionary*, s.vv. “arbiter” (first “a spectator, beholder, hearer, an eye-witness, a witness,” then the judicial sense of one appointed to inquire into a cause and settle it) and “arbitror.” The second entry gives the construction *fidem alicui arbitrari*, “to adjudge, i.e. to give, credit to one,” citing Plautus, *Bacchides* 3.6.41. The line, collated in Friedrich Leo’s text (*Plauti Comoediae*, vol. 1 [Weidmann, 1895], line 570), reads *Postremo, si pergis parvam mihi fidem arbitrarier*, so the lexicon’s formula is a lemmatised form of the attested phrase.

[^s01-m03-s01-arbitration]: The analysis of criterion, delineation and arbitration, and the sentence on arbitration and tacit trust, are the author’s.

#### #3 · The Formal-Limit Genealogy

[^s01-m04-s01-principia]: Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell, *Principia Mathematica*, 3 vols. (Cambridge University Press, 1910–13), vol. 1, preface, pp. v–viii (the 1910 preface, reprinted in the 2nd ed. of 1925, from which the pages are given). The aim and method of the work: v–vi. The chief reason for accepting any theory of the principles of mathematics being inductive, in that it enables us to deduce ordinary mathematics: v. The months of work needed to show a hypothesis untenable, the conclusion that some form of the doctrine of types must be adopted, and the particular form advocated not being logically indispensable, so that little of the book would change with another: vii. The symbolism developed in practice and in large part new because the ideas had not been symbolised before: vii–viii.

[^s01-m04-s01-russell-faith]: Bertrand Russell, “Reflections on My Eightieth Birthday,” in *Portraits from Memory and Other Essays* (Simon and Schuster, 1956), 54; the sentence on “some twenty years of very arduous toil” and the conclusion that nothing more could be done to make mathematical knowledge indubitable follows at 55. Pages are those of the American edition; the British edition (Allen & Unwin, 1956) is paginated differently.

[^s01-m04-s01-frege]: Gottlob Frege, *Grundgesetze der Arithmetik, begriffsschriftlich abgeleitet*, 2 vols. (Hermann Pohle, 1893–1903), 1:36 (§20), Basic Law V, which states that the value-range of one function coincides with that of another just when the two functions agree at every argument. The essay’s paraphrase, that any clearly stated condition gathers a collection, is the form of the principle that Russell’s argument uses. Bertrand Russell to Gottlob Frege, June 16, 1902, and Frege to Russell, June 22, 1902, in *From Frege to Gödel: A Source Book in Mathematical Logic, 1879–1931*, ed. Jean van Heijenoort (Harvard University Press, 1967), 124–25 and 127–28. Frege’s appendix to vol. 2, headed “Nachwort” and dated October 1902, *Grundgesetze*, 2:253–65. On the failure of Frege’s attempted repair and his later papers, see Edward N. Zalta, “Gottlob Frege,” *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*, https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/frege/. The library-catalogue illustration is the author’s.

[^s01-m04-s01-russell]: Bertrand Russell, “Mathematical Logic as Based on the Theory of Types,” *American Journal of Mathematics* 30, no. 3 (1908): 237, §IV, “The Hierarchy of Types,” https://doi.org/10.2307/2369948. The theory is carried into Whitehead and Russell, *Principia Mathematica*, vol. 1, 2nd ed. (Cambridge University Press, 1925), introduction, chap. 2, “The Theory of Logical Types,” 37 ff.

[^s01-m04-s01-whitehead-concreteness]: Alfred North Whitehead, *Science and the Modern World* (Macmillan, 1925), chap. 3, “The Century of Genius,” 74–75, where the error of mistaking the abstract for the concrete is first named the “Fallacy of Misplaced Concreteness”; see also 82 and, at the head of chap. 4, 85.

[^s01-m04-s01-whitehead-smw]: Whitehead, *Science and the Modern World*, chap. 12, “Religion and Science,” 267 (the contradiction sentence). The hypothetical of a doctrine prized as the foundation of a district’s social order, and the question whether the disclosure of discordant results may be forbidden: 266. The theory that is easy to find if one is content to disregard half the evidence: 268.

[^s01-m04-s01-whitehead-halftruths]: Alfred North Whitehead, *Dialogues of Alfred North Whitehead*, as recorded by Lucien Price (Little, Brown, 1954; repr., David R. Godine, 2001), prologue. Price reconstructed the conversations from memory, so the wording is his record.

[^s01-m04-s01-jung-paradox]: C. G. Jung, *Psychology and Alchemy*, 2nd ed., trans. R. F. C. Hull, Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 12 (Princeton University Press, 1980), ¶18 for the two quoted sentences on paradox and Tertullian’s avowal, and ¶19 for the remark on Tertullian’s strength to sustain paradox and the religious certainty it gave him.

[^s01-m04-s01-jung-fossil]: Compare C. G. Jung, “Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious,” in *The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious*, 2nd ed., trans. R. F. C. Hull, Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 9, pt. 1 (Princeton University Press, 1969), ¶11, where Jung says constant usage polishes the Christian mysteries smooth until they stiffen into objects of belief, and that the eternal images, embedded in a system of thought and an institution, shield against immediate experience. The figure of the seal on the tomb is the author’s.

[^s01-m04-s01-whitehead-pr]: Alfred North Whitehead, *Process and Reality: An Essay in Cosmology*, corrected ed., ed. David Ray Griffin and Donald W. Sherburne (Free Press, 1978), 21 (pt. 1, chap. 2, “The Category of the Ultimate”; Macmillan, 1929, 32). On Spinoza’s one substance and its modes, and the philosophy of organism as closely allied to it, 6–7 (pt. 1, chap. 1, §2; Macmillan, 1929, 10–11). Reading Whitehead’s gap in Spinoza as the question of how the many acquire actual existence within the unity is the author’s.

[^s01-m04-s01-spencerbrown]: G. Spencer-Brown, *Laws of Form* (Allen & Unwin, 1969), chap. 11, “Equations of the second degree,” 57–58, where an expression that re-enters itself is given an imaginary state, a state of time rather than of space. In the preface to the first American edition (Julian Press, 1972), vii–viii, Spencer-Brown calls the theory of types a mistaken rule for excluding self-referential paradoxes that are no worse than similar cases already accepted in mathematics, and reports Russell’s remark that the theory was a stopgap. Reading the re-entering mark as the turn `5→0` is the author’s.

[^s01-m04-s01-dycz]: Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, *The Doctrine of Vibration: An Analysis of the Doctrines and Practices of Kashmir Shaivism* (Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 2000), 81, where “subtle movement” is Abhinavagupta’s gloss as Dyczkowski gives it; for the ninth-century origin of the Spanda school and Kallaṭa’s commentary, 21. Page numbers are those of the 2000 Motilal reprint. The comparison with Whitehead’s primordial and consequent natures is the author’s.

[^s01-m04-s01-dycz-three]: Dyczkowski, *Doctrine of Vibration*, chap. 3, “Spanda: The Universal Activity of Absolute Consciousness,” section “Three Moments in the Vibration of Consciousness,” 89–90 (will, knowledge and action; beginning, middle and end), and the section on the conative power, 90–96, where the first moment of the will coincides with its last (91); the closing quotation is at 80. The reading of the triad as `0/1` and its comparison with concrescence are the author’s.

[^s01-m04-s01-jung-logos-eros]: C. G. Jung, *Mysterium Coniunctionis*, 2nd ed., trans. R. F. C. Hull, Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 14 (Princeton University Press, 1977), ¶224. In ¶225 Jung discusses exceptions to his scheme; reading Logos and Eros as two operations performed together is the author’s continuation, distinct from Jung’s gendered account.

[^s01-m04-s01-lacan-drive]: Jacques Lacan, *The Four Fundamental Concepts of Psycho-Analysis*, ed. Jacques-Alain Miller, trans. Alan Sheridan (Hogarth Press, 1977), chap. 13, “The Deconstruction of the Drive,” and chap. 14, “The Partial Drive and Its Circuit” (from 174).

[^s01-m04-s01-savoir]: Charlton T. Lewis and Charles Short, *A Latin Dictionary* (Clarendon Press, 1879), s.vv. “sapio” (“to taste, savor”; transferred, “to have good taste, i.e. to have sense or discernment; to be sensible, discreet, prudent, wise”), “sapor” (“a taste, relish, flavor, savor”). French *savoir* descends from *sapere*: ATILF, *Trésor de la langue française informatisé* (TLFi), s.v. “savoir” (verbe), Étymologie et historique, derives it from popular Latin *sapēre* (a reconstructed form), altered from classical *sapere*, “to have flavour” and “to have discernment, be wise,” which used transitively displaced *scire*; Old French *savoir* kept the senses “to feel” and “to please” into the fourteenth century. TLFi, s.v. “saveur,” derives *saveur* from Latin *sapor*. English *savour* comes through Old French *savour* from *sapor*: *The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language*, 5th ed., s.v. “savor”; Harper, *Online Etymology Dictionary*, s.v. “savor.”

[^s01-m04-s01-godel]: Kurt Gödel, “Über formal unentscheidbare Sätze der *Principia Mathematica* und verwandter Systeme I,” *Monatshefte für Mathematik und Physik* 38, no. 1 (1931): 173–98, nn. 2 (p. 173) and 46 (p. 190), https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01700692. Note 2 names *Principia Mathematica* (2nd ed., 1925) as the system and lists the axioms counted with it (infinity, reducibility, choice); note 46 makes the existence of consistent but not ω-consistent systems depend on the consistency of the system.

[^s01-m04-s01-gap]: The concept of the immutable gap is the author’s. Its application to the strengthening of theories does not claim that a theorem about one class of formal systems proves every closed totality impossible.

[^s01-m04-s01-cusa-polygon]: Nicholas of Cusa, *On Learned Ignorance*, trans. Jasper Hopkins, 2nd ed., 2nd printing (Arthur J. Banning Press, 1990), I.3.10, 8. The bracketed insertions are Hopkins’s. The comparison with the strengthening of theories and with the torus is the author’s.

[^s01-m04-s01-aphorism]: The aphorism is the author’s, as is the reading of Gödel’s sentence as an approachable limit; an unprovable sentence warrants no unrelated belief.

[^s01-m04-s01-wittgenstein]: Ludwig Wittgenstein, *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus*, trans. F. P. Ramsey, ed. C. K. Ogden (Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner & Co., 1922), props. 4.1212, 6.54, 7.

[^s01-m04-s01-tractatus-subject]: Wittgenstein, *Tractatus*, props. 5.632 (quoted in the Ramsey–Ogden wording of 1922; later translations differ slightly), 5.633 (the eye and the field of sight); on the ladder, 6.54.

[^s01-m04-s01-gelassenheit]: Martin Heidegger, “Memorial Address,” in *Discourse on Thinking*, trans. John M. Anderson and E. Hans Freund (New York: Harper & Row, 1966), 54, where the translators’ note records the older use of *Gelassenheit* by the German mystics, Meister Eckhart among them. In “Conversation on a Country Path about Thinking,” in the same volume, 61–62, Eckhart is named as a master from whom much can be learned, while the releasement sought there is set apart from his.

[^s01-m04-s01-golden-flower]: C. G. Jung, “Commentary on *The Secret of the Golden Flower*,” in *Alchemical Studies*, trans. R. F. C. Hull, Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 13 (Princeton University Press, 1983), ¶20, where Jung glosses *wu wei* as action through non-action and links letting go of oneself with Meister Eckhart. The passage is Jung’s commentary, not the Chinese text.

[^s01-m04-s01-lacan-identification]: Jacques Lacan, “L’identification,” seminar 9 (1961–62), unpublished; cited from Cormac Gallagher’s unofficial translation from the unedited French typescripts, privately circulated (lacaninireland.com), 119–23 (session of 7 March 1962, introducing the torus, its full circuits of repeated demand and the empty circle around the central hole), 134–36 (14 March 1962) and 181–85 (11 April 1962). Lacan relates the empty circle to the object of desire rather than to desire itself; the phrase “the desire traced through their repetition” is the author’s gloss.

[^s01-m04-s01-numinous]: C. G. Jung, *Psychology and Religion: West and East*, 2nd ed., trans. R. F. C. Hull, Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 11 (Princeton University Press, 1969), ¶6, where Jung attributes the term to Rudolf Otto, *The Idea of the Holy*, trans. John W. Harvey (Oxford University Press, 1923); the CW 11 bibliography lists the fourth impression of this translation (Oxford, 1926). On the feeling-toned complex, see Jung, “A Review of the Complex Theory,” in *The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche*, 2nd ed., trans. R. F. C. Hull, Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 8 (Princeton University Press, 1975), ¶201.

[^s01-m04-s01-van-eenwyk]: John R. Van Eenwyk, *Archetypes & Strange Attractors: The Chaotic World of Symbols* (Inner City Books, 1997). The use of the basin of attraction to contrast the complex with the symbol is the author’s gloss on Van Eenwyk’s treatment of complexes and symbols.

[^s01-m04-s01-god-image]: Jung, *Psychology and Religion*, ¶¶144–48 (projections withdrawn from the God-image; where the risen Christ is to be found); on the limit between a psychological image and an ontological proof, ¶102.

[^s01-m04-s01-zero]: The crossed zero is the author’s notation, proposed here from the sequence of formal limits alone; its historical and mathematical life is taken up in §1 and §3.

[^s01-m04-s01-nietzsche]: Friedrich Nietzsche, *Thus Spoke Zarathustra*, pt. 2, “On Self-Overcoming,” in *The Portable Nietzsche*, ed. and trans. Walter Kaufmann (New York: Viking Press, 1954). In this speech Life says that she is that which must always overcome herself. The question that follows is the author’s.

[^s01-m04-s01-derrida]: Jacques Derrida, “Différance,” in *Margins of Philosophy*, trans. Alan Bass (University of Chicago Press, 1982), 8 (the two senses of *différer*) and 11 (the signified concept never present in itself; every concept inscribed in a chain or system of differences), within 1–27. “No final signified” is the essay’s paraphrase.

[^s01-m04-s01-pi]: Ludwig Wittgenstein, *Philosophical Investigations*, trans. G. E. M. Anscombe, P. M. S. Hacker, and Joachim Schulte, rev. 4th ed. by P. M. S. Hacker and Joachim Schulte (Wiley-Blackwell, 2009), §§198–202, esp. §201. The regress of interpretations is in §198 and §201, and the way of grasping a rule that is exhibited in obeying and going against it is in §201. The wording of the sentence is the author’s paraphrase.

[^s01-m04-s01-descartes-sailor]: René Descartes, *Meditations on First Philosophy*, in *The Philosophical Writings of Descartes*, vol. 2, trans. John Cottingham, Robert Stoothoff, and Dugald Murdoch (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1984), Meditation VI, 56 (AT VII 81). The sailor who perceives by sight that something in his ship is broken is Descartes’s own comparison, in the same sentence.

[^s01-m04-s01-blindspot]: Adam Frank, Marcelo Gleiser, and Evan Thompson, *The Blind Spot: Why Science Cannot Ignore Human Experience* (MIT Press, 2024): “An Introduction to the Blind Spot,” where the authors name direct experience, the precondition of observation and measurement, as what science leaves unseen, and chap. 1, “The Surreptitious Substitution,” on the reversal of the dependence of the abstract on the concrete. The reading of that reversal as a reversal of Descartes’s order of inquiry is the author’s.

[^s01-m04-s01-chalmers]: David J. Chalmers, “Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness,” *Journal of Consciousness Studies* 2, no. 3 (1995): 200–219, https://consc.net/papers/facing.html, §2 (“The easy problems and the hard problem”) and §3 (“Functional explanation”); §4 (“Some case-studies”) treats neural correlates. Section numbers refer to the author’s online text; §6 (“Nonreductive explanation”) and §7 (“Outline of a theory of consciousness”) continue the inquiry into nonreductive principles. The step from neural correlates to the Subject is the author’s.

[^s01-m04-s01-carter]: Brandon Carter, “Large Number Coincidences and the Anthropic Principle in Cosmology,” in *Confrontation of Cosmological Theories with Observational Data*, ed. M. S. Longair, IAU Symposium 63 (Reidel, 1974), 291–98, at 291, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0074180900235638: what we can expect to observe is “restricted by the conditions necessary for our presence as observers.”

[^s01-m04-s01-neurophenomenology]: Francisco J. Varela, “Neurophenomenology: A Methodological Remedy for the Hard Problem,” *Journal of Consciousness Studies* 3, no. 4 (1996): 330–49. For the direction from experience to experiment, see Antoine Lutz and Evan Thompson, “Neurophenomenology: Integrating Subjective Experience and Brain Dynamics in the Neuroscience of Consciousness,” *Journal of Consciousness Studies* 10, nos. 9–10 (2003): 33, 48, which says that neuroscience has focused mainly on the third-person side and that first-person data should constrain the analysis and interpretation of physiological data; the wording “usually neglected” is the author’s gloss.

[^s01-m04-s01-bache]: Christopher M. Bache, *LSD and the Mind of the Universe: Diamonds from Heaven*, foreword by Ervin Laszlo (Park Street Press, 2019), on his seventy-three high-dose LSD sessions over twenty years. Jung tells the Siegfried dream in C. G. Jung, *Memories, Dreams, Reflections*, recorded and ed. Aniela Jaffé, trans. Richard Winston and Clara Winston, rev. ed. (Vintage Books, 1989), chap. 6, “Confrontation with the Unconscious.”

[^s01-m04-s01-kekule]: August Kekulé, address at the Benzolfest, Berlin, March 11, 1890, in Gustav Schultz, “Bericht über die Feier der Deutschen Chemischen Gesellschaft zu Ehren August Kekulé’s,” *Berichte der Deutschen Chemischen Gesellschaft* 23 (1890): 1302–11; English translation in O. Theodor Benfey, “August Kekulé and the Birth of the Structural Theory of Organic Chemistry in 1858,” *Journal of Chemical Education* 35, no. 1 (1958): 21–23. The account is retrospective, told twenty-five years after the 1865 benzene paper.

[^s01-m04-s01-tesla]: Nikola Tesla, “My Inventions,” pt. 1, “My Early Life,” *Electrical Experimenter* 6, no. 10 (February 1919): 744: “When I get an idea I start at once building it up in my imagination. I change the construction, make improvements and operate the device in my mind.” The series ran in six parts, February–June and October 1919.

[^s01-m04-s01-hadamard]: Jacques Hadamard, *An Essay on the Psychology of Invention in the Mathematical Field* (1945; repr., Dover, 1954), appendix 2, “A Testimonial from Professor Einstein,” 142–43, esp. 143 (Einstein’s reply to question B).

[^s01-m04-s01-keynes]: John Maynard Keynes, “Newton, the Man,” in *Newton Tercentenary Celebrations, 15–19 July 1946* (Cambridge University Press, 1947), 27–34. Keynes wrote the essay for the Royal Society’s tercentenary celebrations, which were planned for 1942 and held in July 1946; his brother Geoffrey read it after Keynes’s death in April 1946. “The last of the magicians” and the remark that the *Principia*’s geometry was “dressed up afterwards” are his; the comparison with the other cases is the author’s.

[^s01-m04-s01-swedenborg]: Emanuel Swedenborg’s journal of April 1743–October 1744 is available as *Swedenborg’s Dream Diary*, ed. Lars Bergquist, trans. Anders Hallengren (Swedenborg Foundation, 2001). His own account of his call and of his conversation with angels is in Emanuel Swedenborg, *True Christian Religion*, trans. John C. Ager (Swedenborg Foundation, 1906), §779; his statement that the natural sciences prepared him is in his 1766 letter to Oetinger (“I was introduced by the Lord into the natural sciences, and thus prepared, and indeed from the year 1710 to 1744, when heaven was opened to me”), quoted in R. L. Tafel, ed. and trans., *Documents Concerning the Life and Character of Emanuel Swedenborg*, vol. 2, pt. 1 (Swedenborg Society, 1877), doc. 208, 139.

[^s01-m04-s01-faggin]: Federico Faggin, *Irreducible: Consciousness, Life, Computers, and Human Nature* (Essentia Books, 2024). Faggin also tells the Lake Tahoe experience in his memoir, *Silicon: From the Invention of the Microprocessor to the New Science of Consciousness* (Waterside Productions, 2021), and in an interview, “Consciousness as the Ground of Being,” by Richard Gault and Jane Clark, *Beshara Magazine*, no. 20 (Winter 2021/22).

[^s01-m04-s01-unknown]: The aphorism is the author’s.

[^s01-m04-s01-hybris]: Henry George Liddell and Robert Scott, *A Greek-English Lexicon*, rev. Henry Stuart Jones with Roderick McKenzie, 9th ed. (Clarendon Press, 1940), s.v. “ὕβρις”: first “wanton violence, arising from the pride of strength or from passion, insolence,” frequent in the *Odyssey* of the suitors; the word is also predicated of acts, among them wishing to be stronger than the gods (Euripides, *Hippolytus* 474–75, where the Nurse tells Phaedra that this is nothing other than *hybris*), and in Athenian law it covers the more serious injuries done to the person. The lexicon’s headline sense is violence and insolence; the overreach of a mortal into an authority not its own is an attested use of the word. The reading of *hybris* through measure is the author’s.

[^s01-m04-s01-phaedrus]: Plato, *Phaedrus*, trans. Benjamin Jowett, Internet Classics Archive, accessed October 4, 2026, https://classics.mit.edu/Plato/phaedrus.html. The Jowett web text carries no Stephanus numbers; they are taken from Burnet’s Greek text as given in the Perseus Digital Library. The palinode begins at 244a, where madness is named the channel of the greatest goods; Delphic prophecy is at 244a–d, purification and initiatory rites at 244d–e, poetry at 245a, and love is announced at 245b–c. Socrates’ recapitulation of the four divine madnesses is at 265a–b.

[^s01-m04-s01-flasch]: Kurt Flasch, *Meister Eckhart: Philosopher of Christianity*, trans. Anne Schindel and Aaron Vanides (Yale University Press, 2015); originally *Meister Eckhart: Philosoph des Christentums* (Munich: C. H. Beck, 2010). The quoted words are the book’s title.

[^s01-m04-s01-jung-know]: Jung was interviewed by John Freeman for the BBC television programme *Face to Face*, filmed at Küsnacht in March 1959 and broadcast on 22 October 1959; the transcript, with the answer quoted, is in *C. G. Jung Speaking: Interviews and Encounters*, ed. William McGuire and R. F. C. Hull (Princeton University Press, 1977), 428. The second quotation, and the original behind our images, of which Jung has no doubt and which is inaccessible, are both in C. G. Jung, “Jung and Religious Belief,” in *The Symbolic Life: Miscellaneous Writings*, trans. R. F. C. Hull, Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 18 (Princeton University Press, 1976), ¶1589 (answer to question 3). On a power unknown in itself, and on conscience, see Jung’s letters of 5 December 1959 to M. Leonard and to Hugh Burnett in C. G. Jung, *Letters*, ed. Gerhard Adler in collaboration with Aniela Jaffé, trans. R. F. C. Hull, vol. 2, *1951–1961* (Princeton University Press, 1975), 524–26 (the passage on the unknown factor, conscience and the God-image is at 525–26, in the letter to Leonard). The letter Jung published in *The Listener* on 21 January 1960 combines these two letters and is omitted from the volume (editors’ note, 524 n. 1).

[^s01-m04-s01-connectedness]: Hannes Kettner et al., “Psychedelic Communitas: Intersubjective Experience During Psychedelic Group Sessions Predicts Enduring Changes in Psychological Wellbeing and Social Connectedness,” *Frontiers in Pharmacology* 12 (2021): 623985, https://doi.org/10.3389/fphar.2021.623985 (an observational, web-based survey, N = 886; communitas during the ceremony correlated with increases in social connectedness, r = 0.25, four weeks after the retreat); Hannes Kettner et al., “From Egoism to Ecoism: Psychedelics Increase Nature Relatedness in a State-Mediated and Context-Dependent Manner,” *International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health* 16, no. 24 (2019): 5147, https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16245147 (a prospective online study, N = 654 at baseline; the increase in nature relatedness depended on the extent of ego dissolution). Both samples were self-selected and both studies report associations; the second paper’s own causal conclusion is not adopted here.

[^s01-m04-s01-jung-individuation]: C. G. Jung, *Psychological Types*, trans. H. G. Baynes, rev. R. F. C. Hull, Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 6 (Princeton University Press, 1976), ¶758 (within the definition of individuation, which opens at ¶757), where Jung opposes levelling down to collective standards and ties individuation to broader collective relationships; and Jung, “Conscious, Unconscious, and Individuation,” in *Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious*, ¶490, where the in-dividual is defined as a separate, indivisible unity or whole.

[^s01-m04-s01-arendt]: Hannah Arendt, *The Origins of Totalitarianism*, new ed. with added prefaces (New York: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1973), chap. 13, “Ideology and Terror: A Novel Form of Government,” 474–79 (isolation and loneliness, 474–75; solitude and loneliness, 476–77; what prepares people for total domination, 478). The clause that loneliness makes the promise of total belonging powerful is the author’s gloss on 478. The earlier sentence on friends and family is drawn from chap. 12, “Totalitarianism in Power,” 431 (a population organised into denouncing its members, in the section “The Secret Police”) and 452–53 (in “Total Domination,” the families and friends of the arrested, and the choice between betraying friends and sending one’s family to death).

[^s01-m04-s01-le-bon]: Gustave Le Bon, *The Crowd: A Study of the Popular Mind* (London: T. Fisher Unwin, 1896), book II, chap. 3, §3, “Prestige”; affirmation, repetition and contagion are §2 of the same chapter. Project Gutenberg, accessed October 4, 2026, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/445. The comparison with media and propaganda is the author’s.

[^s01-m04-s01-bestand]: Martin Heidegger, “The Question Concerning Technology,” in *The Question Concerning Technology and Other Essays*, trans. William Lovitt (New York: Harper & Row, 1977), 14 (challenging-forth), 17 (*Bestand*, with Lovitt’s note 16). “Digitised” extends Heidegger’s account and is the author’s.

#### #4 · Gebserian Diaphaneity

[^s01-m05-s01-gebser]: Jean Gebser, *The Ever-Present Origin*, trans. Noel Barstad and Algis Mickunas (Ohio University Press, 1985), 11–21.

[^s01-m05-s01-heidegger]: Martin Heidegger, “The Age of the World Picture,” in *The Question Concerning Technology and Other Essays*, trans. William Lovitt (New York: Harper & Row, 1977), 115–54. The pairing of Heidegger’s diagnosis with Gebser’s, and the notation of the crossed zero, are the author’s.

[^s01-m05-s01-jorjani]: Jason Reza Jorjani, *Prometheus and Atlas* (London: Arktos, 2016). The reading of the perspectival picture as Atlas’s burden, and of the end of “the world” as the end of a category, is the author’s.

[^s01-m05-s01-jung-prometheus]: C. G. Jung, *The Red Book: Liber Novus*, ed. Sonu Shamdasani, trans. Mark Kyburz, John Peck, and Sonu Shamdasani (W. W. Norton, 2009), 247 (Liber Primus, “Mysterium. Encounter”). Jung writes there that forethinking is Prometheus, who brings the chaotic to form and definition, and that the dark space in which Elijah and Salome live is the space of forethinking; Shamdasani’s n. 168 glosses Prometheus as forethought and refers to Jung’s reading of Carl Spitteler’s *Prometheus and Epimetheus*, where Prometheus is introverted forethought: C. G. Jung, *Psychological Types*, trans. H. G. Baynes, rev. R. F. C. Hull, Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 6 (Princeton University Press, 1976), chap. 5. Jung’s later commentary on the same figures names the old man’s principle Logos, an independent principle of form meaning understanding, insight, foresight, legislation and wisdom (*Red Book*, 365, Appendix B), and in his 1925 seminar he said Elijah and Salome could be called personifications of Logos and Eros: C. G. Jung, *Analytical Psychology: Notes of the Seminar Given in 1925*, ed. William McGuire, Bollingen Series 99 (Princeton University Press, 1989), lecture 11, 89. Jung does not state the equation of Prometheus with Logos in a single sentence; it is joined across these passages.

[^s01-m05-s01-jung-art]: C. G. Jung, “On the Relation of Analytical Psychology to Poetry,” in *The Spirit in Man, Art, and Literature*, trans. R. F. C. Hull, Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 15 (Princeton University Press, 1971), ¶130. The typological reading of artists as led by intuition and feeling is the author’s.

[^s01-m05-s01-aurobindo-gebser]: Gebser, *Ever-Present Origin*, “From the Preface to the Second Edition,” xxix. Ulrich J. Mohrhoff has since compared Gebser’s integral structure with Aurobindo’s supermind and noted differences: Ulrich J. Mohrhoff, “Evolution of Consciousness According to Jean Gebser,” *AntiMatters* 2, no. 3 (2008): 51–78.

[^s01-m05-s01-sarnath]: Gebser’s letter on the experience at Sarnath is discussed by Georg Feuerstein: *Structures of Consciousness: The Genius of Jean Gebser: An Introduction and Critique* (Integral Publishing, 1987). See also Jean Gebser, “Homologies in Spiritual Attitude.” The Śaiva terms *pratyabhijñā* and *samāveśa* are brought to Gebser’s experience by the author.

[^s01-m05-s01-credere]: The distinction between *fides*, reliance already in force before any arbitration, and *credere*, entrustment renewed once an undertaking has returned its consequences, is the author’s, as are the four offices of trust, knowledge, belief and faith set out in an earlier movement of this section.

[^s01-m05-s01-neumann]: Erich Neumann, *The Origins and History of Consciousness*, trans. R. F. C. Hull, foreword by C. G. Jung, Princeton Classics ed. (Princeton University Press, 2014). The thesis that the individual ego passes through the archetypal stages through which human consciousness as a whole developed organises the whole work.

[^s01-m05-s01-functions-mutations]: The alignment of Jung’s four functions, sensation, feeling, thinking and intuition, with Gebser’s magical, mythical, mental and integral structures is the author’s.

[^s01-m05-s01-redbook-origin]: Jung, *Red Book*, 247 (Liber Primus, “Mysterium. Encounter”). The correspondence between Jung’s formulation and Gebser’s Origin is the author’s.

[^s01-m05-s01-jung-child]: C. G. Jung, “The Psychology of the Child Archetype,” in *The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious*, trans. R. F. C. Hull, 2nd ed., Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 9, pt. 1 (Princeton University Press, 1969), ¶299.

[^s01-m05-s01-mana]: C. G. Jung, “On Psychic Energy,” in *The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche*, trans. R. F. C. Hull, 2nd ed., Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 8 (Princeton University Press, 1975), ¶52 and n. 44. Jung draws on R. H. Codrington’s report of Melanesian usage.

[^s01-m05-s01-gebser-arational]: Gebser, *Ever-Present Origin*, 147, where he distinguishes the arational from the irrational and names the pre-rational, the irrational and the rational as its basis. The connection to the paradoxes of the previous movement is the author’s.

[^s01-m05-s01-whitehead-victory]: Alfred North Whitehead, *Science and the Modern World* (Macmillan, 1925), 267 (chap. 12, “Religion and Science”).

[^s01-m05-s01-giegerich]: Wolfgang Giegerich, “The End of Meaning and the Birth of Man: An Essay about the State Reached in the History of Consciousness and an Analysis of C. G. Jung’s Psychology Project,” *Journal of Jungian Theory and Practice* 6, no. 1 (2004): 1–65. The birth of man is argued in §7, “The Birth of Man.”

[^s01-m05-s01-legein]: Martin Heidegger, “Logos (Heraclitus, Fragment B 50),” in *Early Greek Thinking: The Dawn of Western Philosophy*, trans. David Farrell Krell and Frank A. Capuzzi (New York: Harper & Row, 1975), 59–78. On the lexical senses of *legein*, see Henry George Liddell and Robert Scott, *A Greek-English Lexicon*, rev. Henry Stuart Jones with Roderick McKenzie, 9th ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1940), s.v. “λέγω.”

[^s01-m05-s01-bergson]: Henri Bergson, *Time and Free Will: An Essay on the Immediate Data of Consciousness*, trans. F. L. Pogson (London: George Allen & Company, 1913), chap. 2, esp. 100–112, https://www.gutenberg.org/files/56852/56852-h/56852-h.htm. Bergson takes up the free act in chapter 3.

[^s01-m05-s01-bergson-intuition]: Henri Bergson, *An Introduction to Metaphysics*, trans. T. E. Hulme (G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1912), first published in the *Revue de métaphysique et de morale*, January 1903; intuition is defined near the opening. The proximity of Bergson’s intuition to the function that leads the integral structure is the author’s observation.

[^s01-m05-s01-husserl]: Edmund Husserl, “The Origin of Geometry,” appendix 6 to *The Crisis of European Sciences and Transcendental Phenomenology*, trans. David Carr (Northwestern University Press, 1970), 353–78.

[^s01-m05-s01-bratton-lamination]: Benjamin Bratton, *Agentworld: Scenarios for a Preemptive Anthropology of Open-World Centaur Societies* (Antikythera, 2026), 14, §2.5, “Provisional Individuation.”

[^s01-m05-s01-oikos]: Liddell and Scott, *Greek-English Lexicon*, s.vv. “νέμω,” “νόμος.” Ernst Haeckel coined *Oecologie* in *Generelle Morphologie der Organismen*, 2 vols. (Berlin: Georg Reimer, 1866), 2:286. The reading of economy and ecology as the distributing and gathering gestures of one household is the author’s.

[^s01-m05-s01-nomisma]: Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics*, trans. W. D. Ross, Internet Classics Archive, 5.5, https://classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/nicomachaen.5.v.html; Aristotle, *Politics*, trans. Benjamin Jowett, Internet Classics Archive, 1.3 (the household’s relations) and 1.8–10 (provision and acquisition; usury and *tokos* at 1.10, 1258b), https://classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/politics.1.one.html.

[^s01-m05-s01-economy-words]: The derivations of *charaktēr*, *typos*, *legenda*, *token*, *currency*, *value*, *owe* and *own*, *debt* and *interest* are the standard ones. The reading of interest as the pricing of the relation between two parties, and its notation, are the author’s.

[^s01-m05-s01-ephesians]: Eph. 1:9–10. Greek text: *SBL Greek New Testament*, reverse-interlinear edition of Ephesians, https://www.sblgnt.com/download/revint/70-Ephesians.pdf.

[^s01-m05-s01-theologia-oikonomia]: Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, on *dispensatio*; Karl Rahner, *The Trinity*, trans. Joseph Donceel (New York: Herder and Herder, 1970). The reading of the divine economy in the essay’s notation is the author’s.

[^s01-m05-s01-monopoly]: Aristotle, *Politics*, 1.11, 1259a (the story of Thales and the olive-presses).

[^s01-m05-s01-voc]: The Company received its charter from the States General of the Dutch Republic on March 20, 1602, for twenty-one years of exclusive trade between the Cape of Good Hope and the Strait of Magellan; the Nationaal Archief’s description lists its powers to conclude contracts with foreign rulers, build forts, administer justice, hire soldiers and wage war: “Octrooi voor de VOC (1602),” Nationaal Archief, https://www.nationaalarchief.nl/beleven/onderwijs/bronnenbox/octrooi-voor-de-voc-1602 (the charter is Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 1.04.02, inv. no. 1). On the company’s corporate form, see Oscar Gelderblom, Abe de Jong, and Joost Jonker, “The Formative Years of the Modern Corporation: The Dutch East India Company VOC, 1602–1623,” *Journal of Economic History* 73, no. 4 (2013): 1050–76. The characterisation of the Dutch student corps and of the Sicilian Mafia is the author’s.

[^s01-m05-s01-lucifer]: Isa. 14:12 (KJV; Vulgate *lucifer*). C. G. Jung, *Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self*, 2nd ed., trans. R. F. C. Hull, Collected Works of C. G. Jung, vol. 9, pt. 2 (Princeton University Press, 1979), ¶127 (the Morning Star) and ¶68 (the Luciferian development of science and technology).

[^s01-m05-s01-cain]: Gen. 4:1, 4:8, 4:17 (KJV).

[^s01-m05-s01-taylor-antichrist]: The account of the counterfeit economy as un-dual and un-finite, and the figure of the I-Deal, are the author’s.

[^s01-m05-s01-privatio]: Jung, *Aion*, ¶¶74–75. Jung states his position on the plane of empirical psychology, not as a theological or metaphysical thesis.

[^s01-m05-s01-devil-minus]: The formula is the author’s; §2 develops it.

[^s01-m05-s01-aion-antichrist]: Jung, *Aion*, ¶¶76–78.

[^s01-m05-s01-aion-fishes]: Jung, *Aion*, chap. 6, “The Sign of the Fishes.”

[^s01-m05-s01-nietzsche-market]: Friedrich Nietzsche, *The Gay Science* (1882), §125.

[^s01-m05-s01-in-god-we-trust]: The motto first appeared on United States coinage in 1864, on the two-cent coin; it was adopted as the national motto by Public Law 84-851, approved July 30, 1956, and first appeared on paper currency in 1957, on the one-dollar silver certificate, following a 1955 law requiring it on all currency. See US House of Representatives, Committee on the Judiciary, H. Rept. 112-47, 112th Cong., 1st sess. (2011), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CRPT-112hrpt47/html/CRPT-112hrpt47.htm, and Bureau of Engraving and Printing, “History,” https://www.bep.gov/currency/history.

[^s01-m05-s01-schuld]: Friedrich Nietzsche, *On the Genealogy of Morality* (1887), 2nd essay, §4; 1 Tim. 6:10 (KJV).

### §0 — Differentiating Mind

#### #0 · Awareness Bends Toward Display

G. Dyczkowski, *The Doctrine of Vibration: An Analysis of the Doctrines and Practices of Kashmir Shaivism* (Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 2000), 65, 69–71.

The short phrase is Dyczkowski's rendering; the rest is paraphrased.
